source_check.notes: AutoAscend (C01): supported. The organiser report says symbolic bots excelled at keeping the full game state in memory. The NetHack report (read via ar5iv) lists what the agent tracks: non-current levels, monsters, inventory and bag contents, per-level glyphs, altars, shops and stairs. The report does not attribute the win to memory; the authors single out the nutrition strategy as a significant improvement. Kore (C07): the writeup confirms the winner kept, for each board point and future time, a ledger of actual and potential damage for both players. That is a forward model built from known deterministic rules, not a record of commitments with evidence, so mapping it to an obligations ledger is our analogy. The phase framework (defence, attack, expansion, mining, spawning) was inherited from egrehbbt's Kore Beta solution, not invented by the champion. Placings are confirmed (organiser; Kaggle label plus the runner-up's comment). Overclaim: the README line saying AutoAscend wins 'with an explicit state' reads as causal; no source isolates memory as a cause.

cards.already_covered: lab/policies-src/f6-commitment-ledger/f6-commitment-ledger-v1 already implements P01. It rewrites a LEDGER (open, promised, risks, weak, plan) at the start of every take_action note and recovers it with check_latest_logs after a context reset. F1 (f1-steady-balance-v1) shares its base priorities by design, so F6 vs F1 isolates the ledger. The official runner's identity prompt (State recovery section) and its continuation prompt already send the agent to check_latest_logs after compression, so take_action notes are the sanctioned memory channel. The m3 career-risk-review Skill keeps a 'brief current-run assessment'. Not covered: nobody has measured whether a long note is rejected or truncated, or whether check_latest_logs returns notes verbatim.
cards.rationale: The policy content is already folded into F6, and the F6 vs F1 contrast runs inside the family race. A separate target arm cannot pay for itself: at sigma about 12 Y, delta 4 needs about 81 episodes per arm. F6 does depend on an untested interface fact: does a ledger written into notes survive and come back intact through check_latest_logs? If notes are silently truncated or not returned, F6's recovery step is void and its wording must change before any target spend. This can be checked now, through the five official tools, with a few scripted sessions inside the open gate. The token cost is not decisive. A note of about 150 tokens re-read in context over about 170 actions adds roughly 90k tokens per month. That costs at most about 3.6 E-points, about 0.4 Y, and only if baseline use is already near the 500k plateau, far below delta. Transfer is partial. observe already returns the full current state, so the memory need is narrower than in NetHack: open story threads, promises and past feedback. P01's memory rationale also only matters if JiuwenSwarm compresses context or needs continuation prompts within a 48-month run (IDENTITY.md survives compression; MEMORY.md is reset at install). Using MEMORY.md as the ledger store would need clarification, since the rules confine interaction to the five tools; keep the ledger in notes.
cards.experiment: NOW (scripted, real dev, gate open: about 900 of 1,500 sessions used). 3 sessions, purpose 'infra'. In each session, send take_action notes of increasing length (about 200 characters, then just under, at and just over the runner's note limit, then several times the limit) with synthetic ledger text: ASCII, pipes, newlines, no game content. After each action, observe to see whether the state advanced, then call check_latest_logs with count 1, 5, 10 and a large value, and compare the returned note with the one sent. Record in findings.md: accept, reject or truncate; whether a rejected note still applies or consumes the action; whether notes are returned verbatim, and which fields and how many entries come back. Decision it changes: F6 wording (put the most important items first, 'shorten if rejected' versus 'keep it short', and whether to keep 'copy the latest ledger from check_latest_logs'). If notes do not come back, rewrite F6's recovery step before any target run. Not a selection experiment, and no prereg section applies. INSTRUMENTATION (no episodes): the target cost pilot (method-decision section 8) should log continuation prompts and compression events per episode and the months they occur, note lengths and check_latest_logs calls. If no compression or continuation ever occurs in 48 months, P01 keeps only its attention-focusing rationale. POLICY LEVEL (target, when the gate opens): no separate arm. F6 vs F1 runs inside the race (prereg sections 4 and 6), and with about 4 to 10 episodes per family this week the result is an estimate. A cheaper mechanism check is to take logged story-continuation observations from target traces and query the target model with the F6 context versus the F1 context, k samples each, then measure consistency with the recorded promise. That costs about 1 to 2 percent of an episode per probe (prereg section 8.3 probes). If the ledger does not change choices at continuation points, the mechanism is inert for this actor.

source_check.notes: AutoAscend (C01): the competition report confirms a custom behaviour-tree variant whose strategies are non-atomic and interruptible. Its example: exploration is interrupted by combat, and combat by emergency healing. In the author code (strategy.py and agent.py), preempt raises a change-of-strategy exception, runs the preempting strategy, and with continue_after_preemption=True (the default) re-runs the interrupted strategy from its start. That is a restart, not a resume: the plan is re-entered and re-evaluated after the emergency. RAPH (C02): confirmed as neural-track winner, not overall winner. Its rule-based first-fit high-level selector over options hands control to the only learned skill (fighting) based on distance to the nearest monster; eating, exploration and inventory are hard-coded. No overclaims beyond reading 'return to plan' as re-entry.

cards.already_covered: Mode machinery already exists in several families. f3-feedback-reactive-v1 has Clear, Raised and Escalating signal states with a step-down rule after a whole quarter without a new signal. f2-invest-early-v1 has BUILD and CONVERT stages switched on evidence, back to BUILD after a promotion, and CONVERT kept near the end. f4-visible-delivery-v1 has a wellbeing-floor interrupt with 'return to delivery as soon as the trend turns'. The m3 career-risk-review Skill says to return to growth and avoid indefinite defensive play. The statistics side (problem C) is in prereg-v1 section 10 (never and always arms, within-episode randomisation, placebo), method-decision section 3 column C, and the synthetic switch_rule parameter (none, calendar, state, feedback) in careerlab/synthetic/policy.py.
cards.rationale: These are complete-policy behaviours that the initial families already embody in different forms. A separate modes arm, or the 2x2 with P01 proposed in playbook section 3, would duplicate the race at a cost the budget cannot bear. The transferable lesson from AutoAscend is restart semantics: after an interruption, re-evaluate the plan from the current state rather than resume a stale one. That fits an LLM that re-observes every turn. The mechanism is not about search or statistics, so the synthetic testbed cannot say anything about its value for the real game. Its statistical risk (deceptive specialisation) is already designed for.
cards.experiment: No arm. Fold-in checks for every family or child that uses modes (F2, F3, F4, m3, later children). (1) Every note starts with the current mode label and the evidence for it. F2, F3 and F4 already do this; m3 should if it becomes a parent. This makes mode dwell time and oscillation measurable from logs at no cost. (2) Each mode states its entry and exit conditions and says to re-plan from the current observation on exit. (3) Conditions are qualitative and use only state and feedback; calendar or numeric triggers stay diagnostic only (prereg section 10). INFRASTRUCTURE (no episodes): a process-measure extractor over target transcripts, giving mode-label sequence, defensive dwell after the cause clears, and flips between consecutive decisions without new feedback. TRIGGER that would spin off a test: in the posterior leader's target traces, oscillation (mode flips without new feedback) or persistent defence. It then becomes the P08 child below. Any shipped mode claimed as a specialisation must meet section 10: P(mu_switch > max(mu_never, mu_always) + 4) >= 0.8 on fresh games.

source_check.notes: Halite II (C09): the placing is confirmed by Two Sigma (reCurs3 first). The post-mortem, read via the Wayback Machine because the live site refused connections, supports a survival override in 4-player games, an early-game override, a single-target mask whose removal always made the bot worse, and tactical hill-climbing. The early-game mode has explicit exit conditions. The survival mode, however, is explicitly terminal: the author says it does not check whether it could come back, and he is not sure that would matter. So the winner did the opposite of P08's intervention. The case text admits this, but the card still cites C09 as support. Halite's survival mode also existed because 4-player placement rewards having ships at the end, a ranking quirk. AutoAscend (C01) supports leaving an emergency: after the preempting strategy finishes, the interrupted one is re-entered. The counterintuitive claim on the card (less defence when there are no warnings improves the final mean) has no support in any source.

cards.already_covered: Several families already have exit rules. f3-feedback-reactive-v1 steps down one state only after a whole quarter without a new risk signal. f4-visible-delivery-v1 returns to delivery as soon as the trend turns. f1-steady-balance-v1 repeats a main action only while the same gap persists. The m3 career-risk-review Skill says to avoid indefinite defensive play once the reason for recovery is addressed. f2-invest-early-v1 and f1 keep a deliberate end-of-run caution (stay in CONVERT; take no new risks late), the Halite-like terminal mode.
cards.rationale: The trigger (the agent survives but makes no progress) has not been observed. The only real-dev evidence, scripted pilot P1, shows the opposite failure: median survival of 6 to 7.5 months and no completions. Exit rules already exist in F3, F4 and m3, so the race already compares different exit behaviours as complete policies. The Halite evidence cuts both ways. In this game, reaching month 48 lifts the E cap from 50 to 100 and preserves the state counted by Q, so a terminal caution mode late in a run may be correct. Any exit rule should therefore not apply near the end. Under prereg section 10, a modified exit is a mode switch and needs never and always arms to be accepted as a specialisation, which roughly triples its cost. A dedicated arm is not worth target episodes unless the symptom appears.
cards.experiment: TRIGGER: in the posterior leader's target traces (at least 4 terminal episodes), recovery or lay-low behaviour persists for at least one full quarter after its cause has cleared (no active warning, Health and Dignity out of the lower part of their ranges) in at least half of the episodes. Also required: episodes that complete end with weak level or wealth dimensions relative to the survival dimensions. These are lab diagnostics, never Skill text. WHEN TRIGGERED: intervention = the leader plus a public re-evaluation of the recovery reason at each quarter start, returning to growth when the reason no longer holds, qualitative wording only, and not applied in the final part of the run. Comparator = the frozen leader. Outcome Y = 0.8Q + 0.1E. Delta = 4 Y. Episodes: taken from the generate quota (at least 20 percent of slots), 4 for the dormancy check and up to 8 to 12 if it stays competitive. At about 13 per arm only an effect of about 10 Y is detectable, so anything smaller is reported as an estimate. Being shipped as a specialisation adds a 'never exit' arm (the leader without the exit) and a 'never enter' arm, about 4 episodes each, under section 10. Refutation: P(mu_child > mu_leader) < 0.5 after the block, OR relapse (re-entering defence within a quarter) and health- or risk-direction exits increase, OR the manipulation check fails (dwell time unchanged in traces). Prereg sections 3, 4, 6 (Generate, Dormant, Reopen) and 10. Gate: jiuwenswarm-target (currently CLOSED).

source_check.notes: Kore (C07): supported that the winner added an abandon pattern. When a shipyard cannot be defended, the fleet leaves to attack another shipyard, rescue incoming fleets, attack smaller attackers, jump to another shipyard, or retake it later. The version that took the lead on the last day was V127abandonrescuecollideattack. The causal link to the win is not supported. The author says later versions only tuned parameters, ranking convergence was 'a bit unstable', and the lead alternated like 'a game of chance'. Defensibility was computed from exact deterministic mechanics; here viability would have to be judged from noisy feedback among options the game offers. The weakness the case cites (a rival paralysing the first shipyard through a condition in the expansion code) is confirmed by the runner-up's comment. Halite II's survival mode ('abandon at the right time') is another abandonment example, but it served a 4-player ranking rule.

cards.already_covered: m3 career-event-decisions: do not continue a damaging choice only to appear consistent; new feedback can justify changing course. f6-commitment-ledger-v1: act consistently with promises unless new feedback shows the path is harming you, then change course openly and record why. f3-feedback-reactive-v1 weak-review plan: if the next grade is still weak, change the factor instead of repeating the plan.
cards.rationale: Permission to revise a failing commitment is already written into three families. A dedicated arm would test a small wording change at a cost the budget cannot bear. The source mechanism relies on exact computation that this game does not expose, so transfer is weak. There is also a specific hazard. 'Abandon' must never extend to resigning or otherwise ending the run: random play in pilot P1 produced resignation exits, and an early end caps E at 50 and freezes Q at the exit state. The rule must stay qualitative; an 'abandon after N failures' rule derived from dev runs would be a learned threshold.
cards.experiment: TRIGGER: in the posterior leader's target traces, sunk-cost persistence appears in at least half of the episodes. That means the same main-action target or story commitment is pursued across at least 2 reviews after weak (C or D) feedback that names it, or rescue choices are repeated on a story line whose feedback stays negative, while that dimension remains weak at the end. WHEN TRIGGERED: run one combined child with P04. Intervention = the leader plus 'state the current goal, its reason and the evidence that would invalidate it; when the offered choices and feedback show the goal is no longer workable, drop or renegotiate it among the listed options and record the replacement goal; never resign or end the game.' Comparator = the frozen leader. Outcome Y. Delta = 4. Episodes from the generate quota: 4 for the dormancy check, up to 8 to 12 (estimation label). Refutation: the persistence pattern does not fall in traces (manipulation failed), OR P(mu_child > mu_leader) < 0.5, OR early abandonment rises along with new obligations or early exits. Prereg sections 3, 4 and 6. Gate: jiuwenswarm-target (CLOSED).

source_check.notes: Lux S2 (C03): strongly supported by the winner's writeup. Each unit has a role, described as 'long-term but non-permanent', and a multi-step goal. The role is persisted between invocations and checked for validity every step before reassignment. Action selection runs by priority so that low-priority units do not take resources a critical unit needs. Also confirmed: ice-conflict placement accepting worse economic positions, forward simulation, the author's admission that chain-based economies were superior, and the weak matchup against a rival (flg) who moved ice flexibly with heavies. The host congratulated the winner on first place. Kore (C07) supports P04 only weakly: routing is computed 'given an objective', and nothing there concerns persistence or revocation of goals.

cards.already_covered: m3 career-risk-review: hand off a short assessment (principal concern, evidence, next corrective opportunity, growth objective) and reassess after meaningful new feedback rather than carrying an old priority indefinitely. f6-commitment-ledger-v1: a 'plan' slot, re-planned only if new feedback changes the target. f3-feedback-reactive-v1: change the factor if the grade stays weak. f2-invest-early-v1: a stage plus its evidence in every note.
cards.rationale: The Lux mechanism (a persistent but non-permanent role with a validity check) is a good conceptual match. For an LLM, though, it is a prompt-level effect whose size is unknown, and m3 and F6 already contain it almost word for word. As a separate arm it would mostly re-test F6's plan slot. Keep it as the 'persistence' side of the combined P04 and P09 child, activated by a churn symptom, and use the generate quota rather than new budget.
cards.experiment: TRIGGER: in the posterior leader's target traces, goal churn appears in at least half of the episodes: the main-action target or stated priority changes at least twice within one review cycle without new feedback. A lab diagnostic read from notes by the process-measure extractor. The P09 trigger (persistence despite contrary feedback) also activates the same child. WHEN TRIGGERED: the combined P04 and P09 child described under P09. Intervention = goal, reason and invalidating evidence in each note, revised only on relevant feedback. Comparator = the frozen leader. Outcome Y. Delta = 4. 4 to 12 episodes from the generate quota (estimation). Refutation: churn without feedback does not fall, OR P(mu_child > mu_leader) < 0.5, OR persistence despite contrary feedback rises (rigidity). Before spending episodes, a cheap manipulation check is possible: decision-level probes on logged target observations (prereg section 8.3) to see whether the scaffold changes choices at all. If F6 is the leader, P04 adds little beyond its plan slot; prefer P28 or a different family. Prereg sections 4, 6 and 8.3. Gate: jiuwenswarm-target (CLOSED).

source_check.notes: No cited winner kept a register of contradictory hypotheses; the intervention is our invention. HandyRL (C10): the DeNA blog supports the motivating failure. Self-play reinforcement learning learned cooperative assumptions, such as one goose yielding contested food, and these failed against non-cooperative opponents, causing early deaths. The team countered with an ensemble with MCTS that models opponents as possibly aggressive and slightly random. That is search, not an uncertainty log, and the blog mentions no stored hypotheses or uncertainty records. Also confirmed: about 16 million self-play games plus about 3 million against past and diverse models, and a final ranking that hinged on another team beating the rival on the last day. DeNA's own news post confirms first place among 875 teams (the same institution, not independent). AutoAscend (C01) and Kore (C07) contribute state memory and a forward damage ledger, not hypothesis tracking.

cards.already_covered: m3 career-event-decisions: separate explicit information from assumptions about outcomes; update the current-run assessment when the outcome differs from expectations; do not turn one observed outcome into a fixed answer. f3-feedback-reactive-v1: compare what the last choice actually changed with what was expected.
cards.rationale: There is no precedent in the sources, and the motivating failure (optimistic assumptions) is already addressed in m3 and F3 wording. A for-and-against register adds rules and tokens, which raises execution risk for a flash-class target model (problem A) and could cause indecision. Compliance holds only if entries come from the current run. The Skill must never seed 'hypotheses' about game mechanics learned on dev data, since that would amount to unpublished formulas presented as rules. Lowest value per episode in this group.
cards.experiment: TRIGGER: the trace audit of the posterior leader finds the same contradicted expectation repeated at least twice in a run, in at least half of the episodes. That means a note predicts an effect, the next observation contradicts it, and the agent relies on the same expectation again. WHEN TRIGGERED: first a cheap mechanism probe (prereg section 8.3). On logged target observations at the repeated-error points, query the target model with versus without an 'unsure' line (at most two current-run uncertainties with evidence for and against). Continue only if choices change. Then a refine child: the leader, or F6 if it leads, with an 'unsure' slot added to its ledger. Comparator = the frozen leader. Outcome Y. Delta = 4. 4 to 8 episodes from the generate quota (estimation). Refutation: repeated misinterpretations do not fall, OR indecision indicators rise (longer notes, more check_latest_logs calls, invalid actions), OR P(mu_child > mu_leader) < 0.5. Do not add the slot to F6 before the F6 vs F1 contrast has data, since that would confound it. Prereg sections 4, 6 and 8.3. Gate: jiuwenswarm-target (CLOSED).

combinations: Reject the playbook section 3 2x2 factorial of P01 (ledger) and P02 (modes) as a target experiment. The interaction contrast has variance 4 sigma^2 / n, so with sigma about 12 Y, delta 4, one-sided alpha 0.10 and power 0.8 it needs about 162 episodes per cell (about 650 in total). Even the factorial main effects need about 40 per cell (about 160 in total) and assume no interaction. The interaction is not a decision this week; F6 (P01) and F2, F3 and F4 (P02 modes) already race as complete policies.

Treat P02 and P08 as one mechanism: P08 is the exit rule of a P02 mode. Any child tests 'explicit exit and re-plan on exit' on the leader, never as two arms. Prereg section 10 never and always arms are needed only if the result is to be shipped as a specialisation.

Treat P04 and P09 as one child (persistence and revocation are two sides of the same goal scaffold): goal, reason and invalidating evidence, plus permission to drop or renegotiate among offered choices and never resign. Either the churn symptom (P04) or the sunk-cost symptom (P09) triggers it; one comparator (the frozen leader), one budget from the generate quota.

Combine P01 and P28 only as a refine child of F6 ('unsure' slot in the ledger), and only after the F6 vs F1 contrast has data and the repeated-misinterpretation trigger fires. Adding it earlier confounds the only contrast that isolates the ledger.

Shared prerequisite for every trigger in this group, at zero episodes: a process-measure extractor over target transcripts. It records mode-label sequence and dwell time, consistency at story continuations, goal churn, note length, check_latest_logs calls, and continuation-prompt and compression events. These fields should also be logged in the 2-episode target cost pilot. Before any episode-level child, use decision-level probes on logged target observations (prereg section 8.3) as manipulation checks; each costs about 1 to 2 percent of an episode.
review.group_summary:
I checked the primary sources for all six cards in the memory-modes group: the organiser reports (NetHack, Two Sigma), the NetHack competition paper (read on ar5iv because the PMLR PDF was unreadable), AutoAscend's README and strategy.py/agent.py, the Kaggle writeups for Lux S2 and Kore 2022 (read in the browser), the Halite II post-mortem (Wayback copy, live site down) and the DeNA blog and news post. What the cases say the winners did is mostly accurate, with five corrections:
(1) Kore's 'ledger' is a forward map of actual and potential damage built from deterministic rules, not a commitment memory. Its phase framework was inherited from egrehbbt's Beta solution. The abandon pattern is real, but the author calls the final ranking unstable, so no causal credit can be given to it.
(2) The Halite II winner's survival mode is explicitly terminal and never returns to growth. It is a counter-example to P08, not support for it; only his early-game mode had explicit exit conditions.
(3) AutoAscend's preemption re-runs the interrupted strategy from its start after the emergency (restart, not resume). The report never attributes the win to memory.
(4) No winner kept a register of contradictory hypotheses; P28 is our invention. HandyRL countered optimistic assumptions with MCTS opponent modelling.
(5) Lux S2's persistent but non-permanent roles with a validity check strongly support P04.

All six cards are policy-content ideas for an LLM following prose, so none fits the synthetic testbed. Scripted play can only test the interface channel P01 depends on. CareerLab already covers each one:
- P01 is F6 (f6-commitment-ledger-v1, with F1 as the isolating comparator).
- P02 and P08 appear in F3's step-down rule, F4's return-to-delivery rule, F2's stages and m3's risk-review Skill.
- P04, P09 and P28 appear almost word for word in m3, F6 and F3.

At sigma about 12 Y, delta 4 needs about 81 target episodes per arm, against perhaps 20 to 80 in total this week. So no card earns its own target arm, and the 2x2 of P01 and P02 is rejected on cost.

Actions now:
- (a) P01: 3 scripted real-dev sessions, through the five tools, to check whether long notes are rejected or truncated and whether check_latest_logs returns them verbatim. The answer may force a rewrite of F6's recovery step before any target spend.
- (b) P02: keep mode labels plus evidence at the start of every note, entry and exit conditions, re-plan on exit, and qualitative conditions only.
- (c) Build a transcript process-measure extractor and log continuation and compression events in the target cost pilot. P01's memory rationale holds only if JiuwenSwarm actually compresses context within 48 months; IDENTITY.md survives compression and MEMORY.md is reset at install.

P08, P09 (combined with P04) and P28 stay as hypotheses with trace-based triggers. When triggered, each becomes a refine child of the frozen leader inside the at-least-20-percent generate quota, labelled as an estimate, and needs the target gate, which is currently closed.

Compliance is fine in all six cases under these conditions:
- the ledger lives in take_action notes, not MEMORY.md, which would need clarification;
- exit and abandon conditions are qualitative;
- abandoning a goal never extends to resigning, which caps E at 50 and freezes Q;
- P28 entries come only from the current run, never from mechanics learned on dev data.

verdicts.proposed_decision: experiment_real_dev_scripted_now, as an interface probe only, with these changes. (a) Zero sessions first: read the take_action input schema (the notes field) from the official server's tools/list. (b) Then run 1 scripted session, 2 at most, instead of 3. Send synthetic notes of rising length around the runner's known limit of 1000 characters. Record four things: whether the note is accepted, rejected or truncated; whether a rejected note still consumes or applies the action; whether check_latest_logs returns notes verbatim; which fields and how many entries come back. (c) Apply the result to the recovery wording of F6 and also of F2, F3 and both F7 bundles, since all of them call check_latest_logs to recover state. (d) No P01 policy arm. Do not claim that F6 vs F1 isolates the ledger. (e) The proposed target-model mechanism probe needs the jiuwenswarm-target gate and comes out of the prereg section 12 pilot-and-audit share. A probe run outside JiuwenSwarm is a different actor configuration, so it counts only as mechanism evidence.
verdicts.reason: Source check: I confirm the reviewer. The ar5iv paper lists the state AutoAscend tracks (non-current levels, monsters, inventory and bag contents, altars, shops, stairs) and singles out nutrition management as 'a significant improvement'. It makes no causal claim about memory. The organiser report says symbolic bots 'excelled in keeping the full game state in memory'. In the Kore writeup, the ledger is 'actual damage and the damage potential' for each board point and time, a forward model; the phases are 'inherited from egrehbbts solution'. One factual error in already_covered: F6 vs F1 does not isolate the ledger. F6 also adds a joint quarterly plan for Energy and the main action, story rules (close open items, avoid new commitments) and a 'raise results' risk after a C or D review. It drops F1's Act/Watch/Fine classification, its Energy-spread rule and its rule to Lay low only when Health is Act. F6's own policy.json says it isolates 'the ledger and whole-quarter planning'. So no F6–F1 gap can be credited to P01. At 4 to 10 episodes per family the gap's SE is about 12·√(2/7) ≈ 6.4 Y, so it is an estimate anyway. The probe still earns its cost. The limit is known (CAREER_EMULATOR_MAX_NOTE_LENGTH=1000 in careerlab/config.py:25), but over-limit behaviour is not. The synthetic game simply assumes truncation (careerlab/synthetic/game.py:1014, str(notes)[:1000]). F6 puts 'plan' last, so silent truncation would cut it, and F6's 'shorten if rejected' would then never fire. A void check_latest_logs would break the recovery steps of four families. That is a gross execution failure under prereg section 8.1, and it should be found before any target spend. Gate: 752 earlier sessions plus 152 P1 jobs is about 904 of 1,500, so 1 or 2 sessions are negligible. Compliance: writing notes through take_action and checking validation is ordinary development-client testing, not exploiting a loophole; keep the note text synthetic. The token arithmetic (at most about 0.4 Y) checks out. Logging compression and continuation events in the cost pilot costs nothing and is the right way to test the memory rationale.

verdicts.proposed_decision: fold_into_family_design, with these changes. (1) No text edits to F2, F3 or F4. They already meet checks 1 and 2, so the checklist applies only to new children and to m3 if it becomes a parent. (2) Rewrite check 3: ban numeric month or quarter triggers, but explicitly allow qualitative references to the published remaining horizon. F1, F2, F3, F4 and F6 already use such clauses, and so does P08's own 'not in the final part of the run'. Register such clauses as time-aliased modes under prereg sections 3C and 10. (3) Build the process-measure extractor now. It is the shared trigger instrument for P04, P08, P09 and P28. Compute dwell and oscillation from the actions chosen (Lay low, recovery actions, Defuse) and from observe-state trajectories. Use note mode labels only as a secondary self-report.
verdicts.reason: Source check: I confirm it, and I checked the code myself. In autoascend/agent.py, preempt catches AgentChangeStrategy, aborts the interrupted call, and loops back to call func again from its start; until() passes continue_after_preemption=False. So 'restart, not resume' is correct. The paper confirms non-atomic, interruptible strategies (exploration yields to combat, combat to emergency healing), RAPH's first-fit selector, its learned fighting skill, and the switch on distance to the nearest monster. One nuance: the organiser report itself does not describe AutoAscend's architecture; those details come from the paper. Three concrete problems. (a) Check 3 as worded would fail F2: 'So few reviews remain that new capability could no longer show up' and 'Once few reviews remain, stay in CONVERT until the end' are horizon triggers. It also conflicts with the end-of-run clauses in F1, F3, F4 and F6 and with P08's own plan. The linter (careerlab/compliance.py:130–140) flags only explicit 'last/final N months/quarters' patterns and masks the 48-month length, so the lab needs a written stance or the families become non-compliant by its own rule. (b) Restart semantics is already the default of every family's turn loop (observe, then decide, each turn). Adding 're-plan on exit' text costs tokens and buys nothing. Only persistent slots can go stale (F6's plan slot, F2's stage). (c) Note labels are the actor's self-report (problem A), and F1 and m3 write none, so an extractor driven by labels cannot measure defensive dwell across the race. Folding the policy content in, rather than running the playbook's P01×P02 2×2, is still right: at about 81 episodes per arm for Δ=4 the factorial is unaffordable, and the interaction is not this week's question.

verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only, with these changes. (1) Measure the trigger against the policy's own exit rule. F3 steps down only after a whole quarter without a new signal, so a trigger of 'at least one full quarter after the cause cleared' fires on F3's designed behaviour; require dwell beyond the policy's stated exit. verdicts.reason: Source check: I confirm the reviewer on the archived post-mortem. 'Survival mode is a terminal state, it does not bother checking if it could colonize again and make a comeback'. The early-game mode has explicit exits (at least 5 ships; no enemy within 65 units; no orders given). On the mask: 'every time I tried removing this masking, my bot performed worse overall'. Survival mode exists because of the four-player ranking rule. C09 therefore contradicts the card's intervention, and no source supports the counterintuitive claim. A closer illustration sits in the Kore thread, though the card does not cite it: the runner-up exploited the winner's expansion guard 'if incoming_hostile_fleets: continue' and paralysed his growth. That is a defensive guard with no exit blocking progress, but it needed an adaptive adversary that this game lacks, so it does not change the decision. The trigger has not been observed. Pilot P1 had median survival of 6 to 7.5 months and no completions, and the teammate's random batch averaged 5.9 months: the opposite failure. Exit rules already exist in F3, F4 and m3, and the P02 fold-in covers the wording. The reviewer is right to keep late-run caution: reaching month 48 lifts the E cap and preserves Q. The cost estimate checks out: 13 per arm detects only about 10 Y.

verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only, with the reviewer's combined P04+P09 child if it is triggered. Changes: (1) the trigger may fire from any authorised actor's traces, labelled by actor; (2) the 'never resign or end the game' clause should go into every family or into none, as a uniform execution guard, and not only into the child. verdicts.reason: Source check: I read the Kaggle writeup myself and confirm the reviewer. The abandon pattern applies 'If I cannot defend', and its options include 'just leave the shipyard and attack it after its loss'. The leading version was 'V127abandonrescuecollideattack (version 127/146)', which bundles four changes. 'All subsequent versions were variations in the value of the parameters'. The ranking 'seemed a game of chance' and 'The convergence of the ranking seems to be a bit unstable'. So no source isolates abandonment as the cause of the win. The mechanism abandons defence of an asset that an exact computation shows cannot be defended, which is not the same as dropping a growth goal judged from noisy feedback, so transfer is weak. Coverage is real. m3 says 'do not continue a damaging choice solely to appear consistent'. F6 says 'change course openly and record why'. F3 says 'If the next grade is still weak, change the factor'. The trigger has not been observed: there are no LLM traces at all. The resignation hazard is real: P1 had 2 resignation exits in 150 runs, and an early exit caps E at 50. The official identity prompt already says to finish one full game. A guard added only to the child would differ from the leader in two ways at once. Combining with P04 is justified because persistence and abandonment are the two ends of one rule, so the interaction is the question.

verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only, as the persistence side of the combined P04+P09 child, with a redefined churn trigger. (1) Do not count main-action changes: the main action is chosen once a quarter and reviews come every six months, so 'at least twice within one review cycle' is nearly the maximum possible. (2) F1 rotates its main action by design ('Repeat a main action only while the same gap persists'). (3) Story feedback arrives every month, so 'without new feedback' almost never holds. Instead, count changes of the stated priority in notes that no feedback mentioning the affected dimension preceded, measured against the policy's own rule. The trigger may fire from any authorised actor's traces.
verdicts.reason: Source check: I read the Lux S2 writeup myself and confirm the reviewer. 'A role is a long-term but non-permanent job/responsibility'. 'The current role and goal would be persisted between invocations'. Each step, the bot checks 'that the current role is still valid'. Action selection runs in priority order. The author admits the chain-based economies were 'definitely superior', and the flg matchup 'really hurt my final score'. The competition host congratulated him on first place. The reviewer missed some extra support: in the comments the author says he 'really tried to prevent there being too much thrash', and his roles can be 'displaced' by a higher-priority unit. That backs both the anti-churn concern and revocation by urgency. Kore's routing 'Given an objective' is only weak support. Coverage is real: m3 says 'Reassess after meaningful new feedback rather than carrying an old priority indefinitely'; F6 has a plan slot re-planned only on new feedback. A separate arm would mostly re-test F6. No trigger has been observed, because no LLM traces exist. As written, the trigger would fire on F1's designed behaviour, or almost never, so it must be redefined before it can activate anything.

verdicts.reason: Source check: I fetched the DeNA blog and confirm the reviewer. Self-play learned cooperation because 'lucky mutual cooperation earned large rewards', and it failed against non-cooperative opponents. The team's answer was to ensemble with MCTS, assuming opponents are aggressive and slightly random. The blog stores no hypotheses or uncertainty records. Training used about 16 million self-play games plus about 3 million more, and the win depended on another team beating the rival on the last day. The intervention is therefore our own invention, and the card's evidence status should say so. The rest of the reviewer's case holds. m3 already separates 'explicit information from assumptions' and updates 'if the visible outcome or warning differs from expectations'. F3 compares expected with actual change. Extra rules add execution risk for a flash-class model, and slots built from dev data could amount to hidden formulas. The trigger has not been observed: no LLM traces exist. The one related fact on record, the mismatch between log and dashboard deltas, is a measurement hazard, not evidence of repeated misinterpretation.

source_check.notes: C14 (Psyho, AWTF 2025) is supported. AtCoder lists him 1st on 16 Jul 2025. His write-up describes reducing the problem to a single group on a common path with walls, then BFS repair per robot, then a move from hill climbing to SA, a 2s-to-20s time test that gained 25-30% and pointed him at simulator speed, a list of ideas that failed, and a stated preference for simple approaches because they waste little time when they fail. C09 (Halite II, reCurs3): Two Sigma confirms the 1st place and the 29 Jan 2018 close. The post-mortem (recursive.cc) refused or timed out on HTTPS and HTTP and has no indexed mirror, so the claims about phases, the strategic mask with local exceptions and the survival mode that never returns to growth could not be checked. Overclaim: the card links C14 to 'one main priority with few exceptions'. Psyho simplified the problem representation using a lower-bound argument. He did not choose one decision objective, so the policy-level idea is our analogy, not his mechanism.

cards.already_covered: Already in the initial race. lab/policies-src/f4-visible-delivery has one dominant goal (visible Output) with explicit wellbeing-floor exceptions, which is exactly this card's shape. f5-relationship-capital has a single dominant priority (Network/Dignity). f2-invest-early has one dominant goal per stage (BUILD, then CONVERT). They are contrasted with the multi-priority families f1-steady-balance (Act/Watch/Fine on every dimension), m3-teammate and f7. Problem C rules (prereg-v1 section 10) already handle 'wins only in a region, so treat it as a specialist'.
cards.rationale: This idea is a design axis of the families, not a separate intervention, and the family race already covers both sides. A separate structural test (same content written as one priority versus many) would need about 81 episodes per arm at sigma 12 and delta 4. That exceeds this week's whole target budget, and its answer would not change which version we submit. A synthetic test would be circular: careerlab/synthetic/policy.py hard-codes the actor miss rate as miss_base + miss_per_rule x complexity, so simpler policies win there by construction. Compliance is fine if the dominant goal comes from the public docs and the exceptions stay qualitative. Quality risk: a single-priority Skill must still respect every published failure direction, because a Skill that contradicts the game scores 0 on Skill quality.
cards.experiment: No separate arm. Interpretation rule for the race: F4/F5 versus F1/M3 changes both content and structure, so a win says 'this dominant objective works for the target actor', not 'single priorities work'. Trigger for a structure-isolating child: F4 or F5 leads after two blocks, and the design story for the expert review needs the structural claim. Then rewrite the leader's content in Act/Watch multi-priority form (or the reverse for an F1 leader) as one Refine child under the prereg section 6 children cap. Race it in the normal blocks with no extra budget, in estimation mode. Make no superiority claim unless section 7 confirmation data reach delta.

source_check.notes: C08 (Halite 2020, ttvand) is supported by the author's code. The README calls it the winning submission, which is author-reported. In Logic/rule_actions_v3.py, get_config_actions runs these stages in order: update history, then get_ship_scores (high-level task scores), then get_ship_plans (ships sorted by a priority score, contested squares given greedily to the highest scorer), then map_ship_plans_to_actions, then decide_existing_base_spawns. The last step subtracts save_restore_budget and requested_save_conversion_budget before spending on spawns, so critical needs are reserved before marginal spending. main_rule_based.py evaluates configurations against a fixed opponent pool (min_new_iteration_win_rate 0.6). C03 (Lux S2, ry_andy_): the Kaggle write-up did not render (JS-only page), so its text could not be checked. The author's repo README confirms 1st of 646 teams. The code (luxry/agent_act.py) shows a fixed priority order of role actions, with a comment that forge builds take precedence so power stays available. It also runs a forward-simulation loop over FUTURE_LEN steps and has factory modes (Default, Forge, IceConflict) with entry conditions and is_valid invalidation. Unverifiable: that ice conflict 'accepts economically worse positions' and the author's admitted weaknesses. Not mentioned in the card: the winner's code fingerprints specific opponents (opp_is_tigga and similar), which is the analogue of named-event recognition and is prohibited for us. Overclaim: the 'first_line_if_trigger_observed' priority. Both sources are multi-unit bots in deterministic simulators with no isolated causal evidence, while our quarterly budget is only 3 Energy points.

cards.already_covered: lab/policies-src/f6-commitment-ledger: the quarterly plan picks a target, writes Energy actions whose total energy_cost fits remaining_energy plus the intended main action, keeps them complementary, and re-plans only on new feedback. f1-steady-balance and f7-single-skill: an ordered priority list (Act dimensions first, then Watch), and the main action covers what Energy did not reach. method-decision 2.2 lists F6 as 'commitment ledger + joint plan'.
cards.rationale: Reserving the scarce budget for the critical need before marginal uses, and planning Energy and the main action together, is a cheap general procedure that the public quarterly structure supports. It is already written into F6 and, as an ordered priority list, into F1 and F7. The expected effect is small: 3 points, 7 actions, recoverable rejections. A standalone joint-plan-versus-greedy test would need about 81 episodes per arm and could not change a decision this week. Remaining confound: F6 bundles the ledger with the joint plan, so if F6 wins we will not know which part helped. That matters mainly for tokens (E) and for the design story.
cards.experiment: No separate arm. Trigger for an ablation child: F6 is in the top two after block 2, and either its tokens per month exceed the 500k plateau (E < 100) or notes are rejected for length. Then add the Refine child 'F6 without the ledger, joint quarterly plan kept' against frozen F6. Outcome Y = 0.8Q + 0.1E. Token counts have low variance, so the E difference settles in 2-4 episodes per arm, while a Q difference of 4 would need about 81 per arm. Decide by prereg section 11: within delta/2, prefer the simpler, cheaper version. Refutation of the joint-plan component: the execution audit finds plan and executed actions disagreeing in more than 30% of quarters, or no fewer 'needed recovery left unbudgeted' quarters than F1. Uses prereg sections 3, 4, 6 and 11. Gate: target actor (key or self-funded route), closed now.

source_check.notes: C16 (ICFP 2025, Unagi) is supported. The Sakana post (by a participant who works at the ShinkaEvolve vendor) reports 320 trials for about USD 60, fitness = solver time, 2.86 s to 0.44 s (18 rooms) and 127 s to 13 s (24 rooms). The discovered auxiliary variable 'door of A first connects to vertex B' lets the solver decide vertex connectivity before doors, and humans later reused the idea. The organiser prize page lists first prize to MOYOU and Unagi jointly. The post gives no variance or score attribution. C08 is supported as a code architecture separating scoring, planning and execution (see P05). Overclaim: the 'intermediate representation' in C16 is a SAT encoding variable inside a solver. Carrying it over to a prose 'need -> goal -> option' scaffold for an LLM is our analogy, with no evidence from these cases.

cards.already_covered: Present in several families. f1-steady-balance classifies every dimension as Act/Watch/Fine, then decides, with notes like 'act Health; watch Network'. f7-single-skill/three-skills run a risk review before each decision with a note naming the dimensions at risk. m3-teammate career-risk-review hands off 'the principal concern, the evidence behind it, the next useful corrective opportunity and the growth objective'. f6 starts every note with 'LEDGER ... | plan:'. Notes are capped by CAREER_EMULATOR_MAX_NOTE_LENGTH=1000 (official runner env, findings.md).
cards.rationale: Every family except P0 already has a need-labelled step before choosing, in various forms. P0 (none) versus F1/F7 (short) versus M3 (about 1,300 words, the most structured) therefore gives an observational read across the race. A dedicated arm with the card's length-matched control would cost at least two arms of about 81 episodes each for an effect that is probably small and whose sign is uncertain for a small model. It also could not change the submission decision this week. Compliance is fine: writing reasoning into take_action notes is normal tool use and stays within the note limit.
cards.experiment: No separate arm. Trigger: the execution audit on the leader's target traces finds need-action incoherence in more than 10% of applicable decisions, meaning the chosen option's listed status_updates move a dimension that the note marked Act/at-risk in the harmful direction while a listed alternative did not. Then: (1) run a decision-level probe on about 100-150 logged decision points (frozen leader prompt versus leader plus a 3-field note: need+evidence | goal | chosen vs best alternative) and measure coherence change and tokens. Probes inform generation only, never dormancy or promotion. (2) Only if coherence improves by at least 5 points, race the Refine child against its frozen parent in normal blocks (prereg section 6, estimation mode). Refutation: no coherence gain, or tokens per month push E below 100 with no Q gain. Gate: target model access.

source_check.notes: C10 (Hungry Geese, HandyRL) is supported by the DeNA engineering blog. The team ensembled a deep RL agent with an MCTS agent (decoupled UCT, rollouts to game end, opponents modelled as aggressive and slightly weaker) because the RL net does not look ahead and misjudged endgames. The net used about 16M self-play games over 3 weeks, then about 3M more against past models and agents that collide on purpose. Self-play learned to expect cooperation in food standoffs, which caused early deaths against real opponents. Remaining steps are an input feature. The authors say the win depended on another team beating their rival in the last games. dena.ai confirms 1st of 875 teams. Transfer note: the card itself admits the winning mechanism (simulator lookahead) is unavailable here and proposes a different one, a self-check inside the same LLM. External evidence on intrinsic self-correction without feedback is negative: Huang et al., ICLR 2024, report that performance sometimes degrades.

cards.already_covered: Partly covered. f1-steady-balance rules out options whose downside hits an Act dimension and takes no new risks late in the run. f6 avoids options that open new commitments when several are open, and closes open items near the end. m3-teammate career-risk-review says to assess plausibility and severity of downside and not to treat a good immediate outcome as proof that an unresolved commitment is safe. f7 runs a risk review 'before every decision'.
cards.rationale: The documented mechanism needs a generative simulator and state restoration, which the five MCP tools do not provide. The proposed replacement, an intrinsic self-review, has negative evidence for LLMs, adds tokens on every decision, and the card itself warns it may drift towards permanent defensive play. The irreversibility checks already in the families cover the plausible part. Compliance: it must stay inside the single agent (no second reviewer agent, which would breach the single-agent / no-team rule) and use the designated model only. Without target traces showing optimistic, avoidable traps, there is nothing to fix.
cards.experiment: Trigger: in the current leader's target traces, at least 2 of its first 6-8 episodes end, or lose a principal dimension sharply, after a single choice whose listed downside or new commitment was visible at decision time and contradicted the policy's own exclusion rule. Alternatively: the audit shows those exclusion rules violated in more than 10% of applicable decisions. Activation (probe first, cheap): about 150 logged decision points, frozen leader versus leader plus one sentence 'before choosing an option with a lasting downside or a new commitment, check it against the at-risk dimensions, open commitments and months remaining; decide once'. This is restricted to such decisions to bound tokens (combine with P32). Drop the idea if fewer than 5% of applicable decisions flip, or if flips mostly go to Lay low/decline without a visible warning. Otherwise race it as one Refine child against its frozen parent in normal blocks (prereg sections 3, 4, 6; claims only via section 7). Gate: target model access.

source_check.notes: C14 (Psyho): BFS repair guarantees reachability and SA optimises the walls on top, so the 'valid first, then improve' pattern is supported (see P21 for the rest). C17 (Flatland 2020) is supported by the full ICAPS paper. CBS with corridor reasoning failed to scale. Grouped prioritized planning was abandoned for vanilla PP when group size 1 proved most efficient and larger groups gave no benefit. LNS replans neighbourhoods of 5 trains with PP, using three strategies (agent-, intersection- and start-based) chosen by adaptive LNS in proportion to their relative improvement, with 4 priority orderings in parallel. Partial replanning after malfunctions covers only the affected trains. The short SoCS version reports leaderboard gains 282.56 -> 285.36 (SIPP) -> 289.10 (LNS) -> 291.87 (partial replanning) -> 297.51 (lazy planning), 1.16 ahead of 2nd. The organiser report (PMLR v133) confirms the winner was in the OR category. Caveat the card omits: these are sequential leaderboard increments, not controlled ablations. The winning margin (1.16) is smaller than most single increments, so no component is shown to have caused the win. In both cases evaluation was cheap and deterministic, unlike ours.

cards.already_covered: method-decision 2.2 operators: 'Refine' (trace-driven targeted fix), 'New family', 'Wild' on stagnation. lab/policies-src/p0-minimal is the short valid skeleton. Prereg section 6 sets at least 20% new candidates and a children cap per family. Prereg section 8.1 has a cheap-actor execution-failure screen (3 of the first 4), and the compliance linter (careerlab/compliance.py) measures the 'proportion of executable candidates'. method-decision 2.5 keeps 'refine-the-leader' and 'best-of-N' as equal-budget baselines in the planned synthetic method comparison.
cards.rationale: This is a generation-operator choice for the orchestrator, and every piece of it exists already: the skeleton (P0), failure-targeted repair (Refine) and free generation (New family/Wild). A synthetic experiment is not worth building. The parametric SynthCareer policy space has no notion of an incomplete or unexecutable proposal (every theta executes), so it would answer 'local search from a simple seed versus random restarts', which is a different and well-known question. On the target there is no budget to compare generators, since the replication unit would be a whole search. Act on it only when the lab sees the symptom it addresses.
cards.experiment: Trigger: at least a third of the new LLM-proposed candidates in a block fail the compliance linter or the section 8.1 execution screen, or the stagnation rule (section 6) fires while children keep growing in length or rule count. Activation: for the next block, generate children only as 'shortest live valid policy (P0 or the shortest family) + one general repair per observed failure, leaving working parts untouched', within the existing slot allocation (no extra episodes). Judge by the usual race and record the idea origin as playbook:P13/C14,C17. Stop the repair chain and open a new family if three successive repairs bring no gain of delta/2 (the card's own decision rule). The equal-budget refine-the-leader and best-of-N baselines already planned in the synthetic comparison remain the only method-level evidence.

source_check.notes: C13 (Huawei Ireland 2024, acheong08): the README states CP-SAT + Pattern Search and '2nd place' (author-reported). solver/sat.py builds integer buy/dismiss variables for 168 timesteps in one full-horizon CP-SAT solve with a 30-minute limit. It has supply balance and per-datacenter slot capacity constraints, and revenue capped by min(demand, capacity). Demand is a known input, and the objective is revenue minus purchase, energy and maintenance costs. There is no explicit budget constraint: cost appears only in the objective. heuristics.py ranks capacity by expected profit using known demand. The card's facts are accurate, but its framing hides the key enabler: the solver works because demand and the objective are known. In our game the utilities of options are unpublished, and only the costs are public.

cards.already_covered: p0-minimal, f1, f4 and f7 tell the agent to compare energy_cost with remaining_energy and, after success:false, to observe and pick an affordable option. f6 plans the whole quarter within remaining_energy. careerlab/store.py records rejected_actions per episode. findings.md already measures that an unaffordable choice returns success:false without advancing, and that unaffordable two-cost actions can remain listed.
cards.rationale: Exact filtering by published costs is compliant, but in this game it is nearly trivial. There are 3 points with costs of 1 or 2, so a full spend has about 32 combinations at most. A wrong pick is recoverable at the price of one extra tool call. The utility comparison, the part a solver helped with in C13, is exactly what is unknown here. Writing an enumeration into a Skill adds tokens and risks asserting interface facts (for example, whether an action can be repeated in a quarter) that the Skill should read from the listed choices instead. Compliance caveat: no fixed list of 'best combinations' learned from dev runs, and no invented utility numbers.
cards.experiment: Trigger: on target traces, rejected Energy actions occur in more than 1 in 4 quarters on average, or Energy is left unspent while a useful affordable action was listed in at least 20% of quarters. Activation: decision-level probe on logged Energy phases (validity rate and tokens), then one Refine child adding a single sentence ('before the first Energy step, list the affordable combinations that use the remaining Energy, then choose') against its frozen parent in normal blocks. Zero-cost prerequisite now, with no new sessions: scan the 150 existing pilot-P1 scripted trajectories (own run outputs) to check whether the same Energy action is re-offered within a quarter and whether listed costs equal deductions. Then the linter can flag Skill sentences that assert either case. Gate for the child: target model access.

combinations: P05 + P06 as one quarterly-plan module: if either trigger fires, change them together in one Refine child (plan Energy and the main action jointly, within remaining_energy, before the first Energy step). The interaction (enumeration only helps when planning is joint) is worth asking only if both triggers fire; otherwise change one thing at a time. No factorial.

P21 x P22 x P20 (prose length, other group) is the natural structure factorial: one priority vs many, intermediate representation vs direct choice, short vs long. At sigma about 12 Y and delta 4 it needs about 81 episodes per cell, which is unaffordable this week. Use the family race (F4/F5 single-priority vs F1/M3/F7 multi-priority, P0 with no representation vs M3 with the most structure, F7 at about 340 words vs M3 at about 1,300) as an observational read, and claim nothing structural from it.

P27 + P32 (reasoning budget by uncertainty, other group): if P27 activates, apply the self-check only to decisions with a visible lasting downside, a new commitment, or a late-run horizon, so token cost stays bounded and the E term is protected. Probe first, then race.

P13 + P14/P17 (rebuild and restart operators, other groups) are all generation-operator choices for the orchestrator. Evaluate them only through the already-planned equal-budget synthetic method comparison (refine-the-leader, best-of-N), not with target arms. In real use, switch operators on their triggers within the normal slot allocation.

Shared infrastructure that fires these triggers (infrastructure_change_now; no experiment, no new sessions): add to the execution audit, computed from own trajectories, (a) rejected actions by phase, (b) Energy left unspent at phase end while an affordable action was listed, (c) agreement between F6's written 'plan:' and the actions executed, (d) need-action coherence (note-marked at-risk dimension vs the chosen option's listed status_updates), (e) choices with a visible lasting downside or new commitment in the last 6 months. Also scan the 150 pilot-P1 scripted trajectories for Energy-phase interface facts, so Skill wording cannot contradict the game.
review.group_summary: Planning-representation group (P05, P06, P13, P21, P22, P27). Sources checked against primary material: Lux S2 winner code (the Kaggle write-up itself would not render), ttvand's Halite code, the Huawei Ireland CP-SAT repository, Psyho's write-up and AtCoder's ranking page, the full Flatland ICAPS paper plus its short version and the organiser report, Sakana's Unagi post and the ICFP prize page, and DeNA's HandyRL blog and announcement. The case facts largely hold. Two gaps remain: the Halite II post-mortem was unreachable, and the Lux S2 write-up text could not be read. The recurring overclaim is in the transfers. They carry mechanisms out of solver or multi-unit-bot internals, which had cheap deterministic evaluators (SAT auxiliary variables, CP-SAT with known demand, simulator lookahead), into prose guidance for one LLM agent with unknown utilities. Huawei's CP-SAT relied on known demand. Flatland's component gains are sequential leaderboard increments, not ablations. The winning Lux code also fingerprinted specific opponents, an analogue of the prohibited named-event recognition. Decisions: P21, P05 and P22 are already part of the initial families (F4/F5/F2 vs F1/M3/F7, F6's joint quarterly plan, and the need-labelled notes in F1/F7/M3/F6), so the family race tests them and they need no separate arms. P27, P13 and P06 stay hypotheses, each with a trace-based trigger. None qualifies for a standalone target experiment: at sigma about 12 Y and delta 4, n is about 81 episodes per arm, more than this week's entire target budget, and none would change the submission choice. None qualifies for the synthetic testbed either. Its actor model hard-codes a miss rate that grows with complexity, so P21 would be circular there, and its parametric policies cannot represent P13's unexecutable proposals. When a trigger fires, the cheapest path is a decision-level probe with the designated model on logged observations (informing generation only), then one Refine child raced against its frozen parent in the normal blocks. The one useful change now is the shared execution-audit metrics plus the zero-session scan of existing pilot trajectories. verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only. Make no change to the families and do not credit the playbook. F4, F5 and F2 already have the dominant-priority-with-floor shape as independent seeds: their policy.json files say 'change: initial family seed' and record no idea_origin. Drop the structure-isolating Refine child. Trigger, using only existing child slots: (a) a multi-priority leader (F1/F6/F7/M3) whose target-trace audit shows, in more than 10% of quarterly decisions, that it moved the Energy/main-action target between Act dimensions with no new feedback, or picked an action whose listed status_updates lower a dimension its own note marked Act. Response: one Specialise child with a single dominant objective plus qualitative floor exceptions, derived from the leader. (b) A dominant-priority leader (F4/F5) that ignores a breached floor in more than 10% of applicable quarterly decisions (listed status_updates lower the breached dimension while a listed alternative did not). verdicts.reason:
Sources, re-checked. Psyho's approach.md says he 'always use[s] a single group' with a 'fixed path for the whole group', and BFS repair then hill climbing then SA. The 20s-versus-2s test gave 25-30%. He states 'I always go for simple solutions, because it allows me to iterate more quickly.' He never describes a single decision objective with exceptions. recursive.cc refused the connection again (ECONNREFUSED), this fetch tool blocks web.archive.org, and a search found no mirror. So C09 is still unverified, and neither cited source supports the card's mechanism. The reviewer's source check, transfer verdict and circularity argument are correct. careerlab/synthetic/policy.py lines 14-16 and complexity() count active conditional rules, so a synthetic test would reward simplicity by construction. review.group_summary: The six search-stagnation cards borrow from contests with cheap, deterministic or full-information evaluators: Flatland LNS (up to 10,000 iterations per instance, deterministic flowtime), the AHC058 solver's internal SA, Huawei Ireland SA after a 1000x evaluator speed-up, RPS bandits that score every expert against the revealed opponent move, and Lux RL over 20B steps. The primary sources support what the winners did, with five overclaims. (1) AHC058's large rebuild neighbourhoods are inside the submitted program; ALE-Agent's outer loop, our analogue, selects the best. Sakana's 'contributed significantly' is its own unablated analysis. (2) C15 does not support P18. (3) No source shows population-level stepping stones (P16). (4) C05 barely supports P17. (5) C11's selectors depend on counterfactual updates we cannot have. Kore adds a sobering datum: an expert's diagnosis-driven changes needed 26 updates over two weeks to beat his own V92. A rough simulation of the coded protocol at this week's budget (20-80 target episodes, sigma about 12) found two statistical problems. First, the score-based stagnation trigger cannot separate improving from stalled search: it fires 0.46 when children truly gain Delta versus 0.70 when they lose 2. Second, dormancy at n=4 against a winner's-cursed leader fires in most runs; with small between-family spread, about a quarter of dormancies hit arms truly within Delta, and the true best goes dormant in 3-5% of runs before audits. Neither reaches the target. Decisions: no target experiment for any card, since operator comparisons need many complete searches. One zero-cost synthetic study (P16, also covering P19's comparator and the stall trigger) to settle prereg v2 before racing starts. P17 folded into the families via observed-behaviour descriptors and merging of behavioural duplicates. P15 and P18 merged into one metadata and diagnosis-check change. P14 and P19 kept as hypotheses with explicit trace-level or budget triggers. All six are compliant: they are lab-side procedures, and any resulting Skill text still passes the linter (no event answers or thresholds). Sources were read in full where accessible; the two Kaggle writeups were read through the browser pane. The Huawei official results page (S35) and the S22 code file were not re-checked.

A three-arm test (adaptive, uniform brief, uniform long) on target episodes is unaffordable, and the effect on Q is unknown and probably below detection.
