Check triage accuracy on the P26 probe battery first (does the model flag the right items?), then race the child against the frozen leader on Y under §3-§6 and §11: 4-8 target episodes, estimation label, Delta 4, gate jiuwenswarm-target. Refute it if the child's completion rate or posterior mean Y falls below the leader's by Delta/2, or if probes show the flag misclassifies more than a quarter of high-stakes items; then keep the better uniform level, as the card says. Until a trigger fires, keep as hypothesis.

source_check.notes: C10 is verified. DeNA's engineering blog says HandyRL combined a deep RL agent with an MCTS look-ahead agent to cover the RL agent's blind spots: traps, endgame length, and an assumption that opponents cooperate, which self-play had taught. It trained on about 16M self-play games and then about 3M against diverse opponents (past models, deliberate colliders), and it says the final rank depended partly on other teams' games. DeNA's news page says first of 875 teams; that is the authors' own institution. C02 (RAPH) is verified, see P07. Neither case compares actors of different capability running the same policy, and none measures rank agreement or false rejections. The nearest analogue is a proxy evaluator embedding a false assumption. The Halite II post-mortem adds that local testing against previous versions 'became increasingly inaccurate' compared with online results, which supports anchoring on the real evaluator. The card's specific mechanism comes from the lab's own audit, not from these cases.

cards.already_covered: Fully covered as problem A. Selection is anchored on the target (method-decision §1.4, §2.5, §3A; prereg §8). Cheap actors may only screen execution failures, supply traces and answer decision-level probes. Pruning authority requires 8 or more shared policies spanning 16 or more Y, P(rho > 0.5) >= 0.8 and zero audited false rejections, implemented in careerlab/stats.py (calibration, pruning_authority, audit_ipw). Dormant target candidates are audited with q = 0.2 per block (§6). The synthetic testbed already models cheap_capability (misses grow with rule count), cheap_biased (caution) and eager actors (careerlab/synthetic/policy.py).
cards.rationale: The card's comparator, choosing all candidates with the cheap actor alone, is already rejected by the frozen protocol. Its premise is also weak here: Claude Haiku is not cheaper per token than deepseek-v4-flash, scripted actors cannot execute language Skills, and Claude actors on the real game are closed by the gate. A synthetic study would only recover the capability bias the testbed was built with (miss_per_rule x complexity). The authority rule is not expected to be met this week, so the study cannot change a decision now. Compliance: using Claude actors on dev games, or on logged dev observations, is not addressed by the rules and is part of the pending organiser question.
cards.experiment: Activate on either trigger: (a) the organisers approve Claude actors on the real game and shared policies exist with target data; or (b) a rank reversal between a cheap actor and the target is observed on any shared policy. Then: start the prereg §8 calibration on shared frozen policies. Prefer the P26 decision-level probe items given to both actors (§8.3) over full Claude episodes. Keep authority off until §8's thresholds are met, and audit any cheap-flagged rejection on the target with logged probability. Zero-target-cost add-on if the build workflow's synthetic method comparison already includes the 'cheap-worker pruning from the start' baseline (method-decision §2.5): run pruning_authority() over replicated calibration studies under the cheap_capability and cheap_biased actors, and report how often authority is granted when cheap pruning raises P(regret > Delta). If that exceeds 10 % of replications, tighten the rule in a v2 protocol before authority is ever used. Do not build a separate study.

combinations: One target probe battery serves P26 (structured versus compact format), P20 (unfollowed rules to subtract), P07 (errors located in one phase) and P32 (triage accuracy). It uses about 40 invented vignettes from published rules only and costs zero game episodes. Probe results feed generation only and never trigger dormancy or promotion.

P20 + P32 become one 'economy child' (subtracted rules, brief by default with explicit comparison only on flagged decisions), and only if the target cost pilot shows token pressure (over 500k tokens per month or unfinished runs). Run no 2x2 factorial: their interaction is not the question, and 4 arms of about 81 episodes each are far beyond the 20-80 target episodes.

P07 + P29: every targeted Refine must pass the decision-time information check before freezing. The cited evidence must be what the agent saw at that step, and the trigger must be stated as visible state, visible feedback or published rules, never as a hindsight or dev-dataset pattern.

P25 + P26: if Claude actors are ever approved, cross-actor comparison uses the same probe items for Claude and the target (prereg §8.3) instead of full Haiku/Sonnet/Opus episodes, and never drives selection.
review.group_summary:
All six actor-capability cards cite case facts that mostly check out against primary sources. One exception: C06 (P29) is unverifiable because the Kaggle write-up does not render. However, none of the cited cases tests the cards' language-model mechanisms. The cases concern trained RL modules (RAPH), bandit selectors (RPS), solver or representation reductions (Psyho, Unagi) and simulator compute budgets (Lux S2, Halite II). The Halite II winner even reports that removing a component always hurt, a counterexample to blanket subtraction. P20's mechanism finds external support in IFScale, but at our instruction density the expected effect is small.

CareerLab already covers most of the group:
- target-anchored selection, pruning authority, calibration and IPW audits (P25);
- structured step families with p0-minimal as the compact extreme, and the gated model comparison of §4 (P26);
- the Refine operator and phase-sectioned Skills (P07);
- the §11 simplicity tie-break (P20).

The cost arithmetic decides the rest. At sigma_Y about 12 and Delta 4, a superiority test needs about 81 episodes per arm, and 4-6 episodes detect only about 15-18 Y. So no card earns a dedicated target arm. Interventions enter as trigger-gated children in the normal generate slots (P20, and P32 via an economy child), or as zero-episode decision-level probes on the designated model inside JiuwenSwarm (P26).

E is insensitive to Skill length and reasoning verbosity: 0.1 Y per 25k tokens per month, and flat below 500k tokens per month. Token economy matters only if runs fail to finish.

Decisions:
- P29: the one change to make now, at no cost. The trace-diagnosis export and Refine metadata must separate decision-time information from hindsight, so that dev-dataset patterns do not leak into Skills, which the rules prohibit.
- P26: experiment on the target when available, rescoped from a Claude cross to target-only probes.
- P20: experiment on the target when available, as a trigger-gated child arm.
- P07: fold into family design.
- P32 and P25: keep as hypotheses with explicit triggers.

No synthetic or scripted real-dev experiment is justified. Claude-actor variants of P25 and P26 stay behind the organiser question.

verdicts.proposed_decision: infrastructure_change_now, with three amendments. (a) Acceptance must cover the target log path, not only CareerLab's own trajectory.jsonl. Add an adapter from the official runner's events_log to decision-time records and accept it on the first 2+2 pilot trace. (b) Build the format-agnostic parts now: the separation function over the CareerLab trajectory schema, and the policy.json provenance fields (idea_origin, cited decisions, hindsight_needed, visible-state trigger), with the linter requiring them for every child. Build the events_log adapter right after the pilot and before the first Refine. (c) Add to the review of every child the rules' invariance test: would the rule stay valid if event wording, order or parameter values changed? A per-episode decision-time view does not stop cross-episode pattern mining.
verdicts.reason: I could not check the source either: the Kaggle write-up fetch returns only the title 'Imitation Learning: 3rd Place Solution', and a search found no mirror. The reviewer is right that the mechanism is plain analysis hygiene and does not depend on C06. The coverage claim holds and is even understated. careerlab/ has no trace-diagnosis export at all: diagnostics.py only checks isolation, and a grep finds nothing for hindsight, decision-time or idea_origin. idea_origin, which method-decision §2.4b requires, is also not enforced: compliance.py POLICY_KEYS lists family, name, parents, hypothesis, change, predicted_behaviour, refutation, skill_count and notes, and unknown keys are never checked. Two defects in the spec. First, its acceptance test uses 'a sample scripted P1 trajectory'. But the traces a Refine will actually read come from careerlab/actors/official_runner.py `_from_report`, which sets trajectory_path from report['events_log'], a JiuwenSwarm runner format nobody has seen because no target episode has run. The test as written would pass while the path that matters stays untested. Second, the real compliance risk is cross-episode pattern mining. The rules warn against assuming a 'pattern noticed in the development validation dataset' holds. A per-episode decision-time view does nothing about that; only item (2)'s trigger restatement plus an invariance check does. The change costs under a day and no episodes, and it must exist before the first target Refine, so the decision category stands.

verdicts.proposed_decision: Drop the structured-versus-compact format A/B and keep it as hypothesis_only. Trigger: in-game audits of target traces in at least 2 families show a rule group followed in fewer than half of the decisions where it applies, and a rewrite would not remove the rubric elements. Replace it with a narrowed instrument, experiment_on_target_when_available after the 2+2 pilot. A comprehension and application probe on the structured arms only: about 8 vignettes per near-limit or post-review rule group of the top 2-3 families, 3 repeats, sent through a client to the slot's JiuwenSwarm 0.2.4b3 instance with the game MCP server removed or unreachable. Output: per-rule adherence and dead-rule flags that feed P20 trigger (ii), P07 children and P32 triage. It never touches Y, dormancy or promotion. Gate: jiuwenswarm-target. The audit's original recommendation (restate the rule, apply it to 5 vignettes, used as a covariate) is the template.
verdicts.reason: Sources: I confirmed the Sakana numbers myself (320 trials, about USD 60; 2.86 s to 0.44 s, 127 s to 13 s; the auxiliary vertex-before-door variable; the idea later reused by humans; 'a genuine team effort'). The page says nothing about instruction structure for LLM actors of different sizes. So the card's hypothesis has no source support, as the reviewer also found. The decision fails on decision value and power. (1) The format default is already fixed by the official rubric (competition-rules: 'The steps are executable: priorities and decision criteria, including what to do near a limit'), and prereg §11 scores versions with 0.1·D̂. A compact prose child that keeps those elements is no longer compact prose: it is a P20 'leader-minus' child, which P20 already covers. (2) The probe cannot make its own decisions. With 40 paired items and 3 repeats at p≈0.7, binomial noise alone gives a per-item difference SD of about 0.37 (sqrt(2·0.21/3)) and a 95 % CI of about ±11 pp. So the 10 pp superiority rule is noise-dominated, and the 'compact ≥ structured − 5 pp' equivalence branch would need about 200 or more items. (3) Timing: it needs 'the leading family', which exists only after at least 4 target episodes in each of 6-8 families. That is about 24-32 or more of the week's 20-80 target episodes, so not before 29-30 Oct, and any compact child would then need 4-8 more episodes, landing at R3 at best. (4) No harness exists. official_runner.py exposes only `career_sim_runner play` against a jiuwenswarm-start ws URL, and that instance has the game MCP server configured, so 'no game tools invoked' must be enforced, not assumed. What is worth keeping is per-rule dead-rule detection. Vignettes can exercise near-limit rules that 4-8 in-game episodes rarely reach, and the rubric rewards exactly those rules.

verdicts.proposed_decision: experiment_on_target_when_available through the normal generate slots, as specified. Amend trigger (i): it should read 'no evidence of gain', not 'complexity without gain'. Prefer to require it after at least 6 episodes each, or together with trigger (ii) or an audit finding, so a noise-driven firing does not take a generate slot from a better-motivated child.
verdicts.reason: I re-checked the sources. The RPS README says verbatim 'delete all of the if-else statements and just keep beta distribution for agent selection'; that it 'dominated over all of my previous agents'; and 'unable to find a consistent way to evaluate my local agent because LB is noisy'. First place is claimed only in the repository title; the README text itself mentions 'Top 5%' in an earlier phase. So the reviewer is right that this is a bandit-selector simplification on noisy feedback, not removal of natural-language instructions. IFScale's abstract confirms the best frontier models reach 68 % at 500 instructions and favour earlier instructions. I could not re-fetch the Halite II post-mortem (live site refuses connections, and Wayback is blocked for my fetcher), so the focus-mask counterexample rests on the reviewer's reading. Coverage holds: p0-minimal is 137 words against 342-486 for the families; §11 tie-break; Refine and Wild operators. The arithmetic holds: 81 episodes per arm, and a token saving under 0.02 Y. The reviewer also did not route this to the synthetic testbed, which is correct: careerlab/synthetic/policy.py hard-codes miss = miss_base + miss_per_rule·complexity, so a synthetic subtraction test would only return that assumption. One defect: trigger (i) is loose. With 4 episodes each and σ_Y≈12 in different families (little pooling), the SD of the posterior difference is about 8.5. 'P(μ_leader > μ_p0 + Δ) < 0.5' fires whenever the observed difference is below 4. That happens about 50 % of the time when the leader truly beats p0 by Δ, and about 32 % when it beats it by 2Δ. It costs only generate slots, so the decision stands with the amended trigger.

verdicts.proposed_decision: fold_into_family_design, with two amendments. (a) The one-section rule applies to Refine only. A Recombine, a Wild change, or a P14-style rebuild of related modules may touch several sections, but must say so in policy.json. A cross-phase cause (for example Energy use that starves the main action) must not be forced into a single-section patch. (b) The before/after phase error metric comes from LLM audits of qualitative rules (Act/Watch/Fine), so double-code a sample with two independent auditors and report their agreement before relying on it. Make target_phase and idea_origin required child keys in the policy.json linter.
verdicts.reason: I verified the sources myself. The NetHack report names AutoAscend overall winner and RAPH neural-track winner, and says the top three overall places were symbolic, with the best symbolic agent 'almost 3x' the best neural one in median score. The paper on ar5iv says RAPH's selector is rule-based and first-fit, that only fighting was learned (TorchBeast; 8 + 8 + 3 = 19 actions), that training used pasted fragments with a hostile monster in view, and that there is no ablation. So the reviewer's 'modular decomposition is workable, not proof that a bounded revision fixes the bottleneck' is accurate. Coverage is real. f1's SKILL.md already has stable phase headings (Each turn, Story events, Quarterly Energy, Quarterly main action, Across the run). tests/test_compliance.py::test_f7_single_and_split_share_identical_strategy_text gives a precedent for a byte-identity test, so the fold-in is cheap and costs no episodes. Gaps: compliance.py does not require or validate the new policy.json fields (unknown keys are ignored). A strict one-section rule would also conflict with the playbook's own P14 and with the method's Recombine and Wild operators if it were applied beyond Refine. Neither gap changes the category.

verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only, as specified. Amend the trigger: a target run that fails to finish counts only if it hits a context or official-runner limit. A run stopped by our own TargetConfig.timeout_s (7200 s, a guess) is a prereg §3 infrastructure alarm, fixed by raising the timeout to at least 3× the measured median; it does not trigger an economy child. Nothing in findings.md or method-decision.md shows the trigger now.
verdicts.reason: I verified the C04 code: agent_act.cpp runs a fixed-priority sequence of ugroup.do_* calls and a look-ahead loop bounded by FUTURE_SIM_PROD/DEV. It breaks when elapsed_time + time_per_step > max_time, gives every iteration the same treatment, and has no uncertainty-based allocation. So 'reserves urgent decisions' is the playbook's inference, as the reviewer said. I could not re-fetch the Halite II post-mortem (connection refused; Wayback blocked for my fetcher). On the lever, the official docs confirm the reviewer: api-key.rst says 'Configure only these three values', and the manifest has only team, name, mode and instruction, so no reasoning-budget setting can be submitted. The E arithmetic is right: 1 E per 25k tokens per month, so going from 500k to 1M tokens per month costs 2 Y. The trigger has not fired. No target episode exists, and findings.md's illustrative 12 M tokens per run is about 250k tokens per month, where E is 100. One risk the reviewer missed: official_runner.py's TargetConfig.timeout_s = 7200 is set before any measured median. Prereg §3.6 requires at least 3× the median, and a 48-month JiuwenSwarm game of about 170 actions could exceed 2 h. Under the current wording that lab artefact would fire P32's 'failing to finish because of timeouts' trigger.

verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only with the reviewer's two activation triggers. Add that the 'zero-target-cost' synthetic add-on depends on the method-comparison component (careerlab/search), which does not exist yet. If built, it should report only the rate at which pruning_authority() wrongly grants authority under the cheap_capability and cheap_biased actors; it is not a test of the mechanism. Neither trigger is observed now.
verdicts.reason: I verified the sources. DeNA's blog describes RL combined with MCTS to cover traps, endgame and the self-play 'opponents cooperate' assumption. It reports about 16 M self-play games, then about 3 M against diverse opponents (past models, deliberate colliders), and says first place came after another team beat their rivals. As the reviewer said, neither case measures cross-actor rank agreement. Coverage is real. careerlab/stats.py implements calibration(), pruning_authority() (k_min=8, span_min=16, P(ρ>0.5)≥0.8) and audit_ipw(). careerlab/synthetic/policy.py defines target, cheap_capability (miss_per_rule 0.07), cheap_biased and eager actors. Prereg §8 already rejects the card's comparator, choosing with the cheap actor alone. The study cannot change a decision this week. Claude actors on the real game are closed in lab/gate.json, and authority needs at least 8 shared policies with target data, which 20-80 target episodes cannot supply. No rank reversal can be observed without target data, so trigger (b) has not fired. The one inaccuracy is that the add-on assumes a synthetic method comparison already exists: method-decision §0 lists careerlab/search as being built, and the directory is absent.

source_check.notes: C05 (Flat Neurons, Lux S3) is supported. The team kept a frozen teacher with a KL loss against forgetting and a pool of older opponents. In the comments, the author adds that the teacher was replaced only when a new model beat it, and that the frozen pool grew to 15-20 checkpoints. New iterations were checked by win rate against older versions and the teacher. C08 (ttvand Halite 2020) is only partly supported. The README confirms the winning submission (author-reported). The fetched main_rule_based.py (blob 9230c0e, matching the recorded SHA) has a branch that promotes a new iteration when its win rate against previous pools and the previous iteration is at least 0.6, and it calls evolve_config. The committed config disables that branch: play_fixed_pool_only=True and num_games_previous_pools=num_games_evaluation=0. It runs a fixed opponent pool with 7 deterministic, seeded games per configuration and an optional skopt optimiser. Nothing shows this harness produced the winning parameters, and its fixed seeds (common random numbers) are unavailable in our game. Two other cases help the card. Kore (C07) needed two weeks and 26 updates before a version consistently beat its frozen V92. Halite II (C09) measured specific failure metrics: docked ships destroyed soon after docking, and final rank against the tiebreaker. Halite II also cuts against the card: its author found that local head-to-head testing against previous versions grew increasingly inaccurate, because of non-transitive multiplayer matchups. Metadata: the claimed comments by the host and by the second-placed player (S05, S10) are not visible now; both pages show 0 comments.

cards.already_covered: Mostly covered. The prereg-v1 section 6 leader anchors dormancy, the archive is reversible, and dormant policies are audited with q=0.2. Section 7 requires fresh confirmation against the incumbent, and confirmation data never feed selection. Section 11 is the submission rule, and content-identical versions are not rescored. stats.decide takes an incumbent. Method-decision section 2.5 keeps refine-the-leader as an equal-budget baseline in the synthetic comparison, and the R3 timeline has confirmation against the incumbent. Not covered: a failure-family regression report against the frozen champion, an explicit champion and submitted-version record with its official score, and a true-regression metric in the synthetic comparison.
cards.rationale: In a single-agent game there are no opponents. The non-transitivity that made opponent pools necessary in Lux, Halite and Hungry Geese does not arise, so 'beat the frozen champion' reduces to comparing means on the same environment distribution. Champion-anchored racing already does that. What CareerLab lacks is the diagnostic half of the card: showing what a candidate loses or keeps relative to the champion by failure family, the way Halite II measured failures mechanism by mechanism. This is cheap. It uses trajectories that already exist (episode.py logs every observation and action), and it feeds expert-review video question 2, which asks what earlier logs showed and how a later version changed. Stage 1 is the maximum over scored versions, so a later version that regresses costs no Stage 1 points. The champion record matters for the final ZIP, which experts read, for the per-version document-quality term, and for any confirmation claim. A dedicated target experiment would change no decision.
cards.experiment: Engineering change, no game sessions. (a) Champion record in the registry: the frozen hash of the best-posterior target policy, plus each submitted version with its predicted and official score when released, kept apart from the research population. The champion stays an arm in every block and is the comparator for promotion and section 7 confirmation. (b) A regression card generated automatically at every promotion or dormancy decision, from trajectories. It compares candidate and champion on exit-cause shares with Bayesian-bootstrap intervals, the Kaplan-Meier curve and RMST to month 48, ending-dimension contributions, review-grade sequence, rejected actions, tokens per month and E. It is descriptive only and never a gate, because v1 is frozen. A failure family that worsens by at least 2 SE gets a written note and may spawn a refine child. (c) In the planned synthetic method comparison, add two metrics: the true-regression rate (share of promotions whose true mu is below the then-champion's true mu) and the lineage's maximum drawdown of true mu. These compare champion-anchored racing with a refine-the-last-version chain at equal episode budgets, as added metrics, not a new experiment. Test the analyser on the existing P1 scripted trajectories. Cost: about half a day of engineering and 0 sessions. Value test: if after two target blocks the card has changed no note, child or video argument, drop it from the routine. Prereg sections used: 6, 7 and 11. Gate: none for building; target cards wait for the jiuwenswarm-target gate.

source_check.notes: C05 is supported. Flat Neurons used a frozen pool of older opponents so the agent would not overfit to a single self-play style, and judged models by real win rates. C10 is supported by DeNA's engineering blog: about 16M self-play games, then about 3M against varied opponents (past models and agents that collide on purpose). Self-play had taught the agent to expect cooperation that real rivals did not give, which caused early deaths. The authors also say their matchup assumptions were too loose during the final evaluation window. The DeNA news page confirms first place out of 875 teams; it is the authors' own institution, not an independent source. Halite II's author also wished he had more diversity in his local pool, and in Kore every version shared one weakness that a rival exploited late. The source mechanism is diversity of opponents during training and evaluation. That differs from this game's environment shift, which is what the card adapts it to.

cards.already_covered: Partly. Method-decision section 2.2 has an archive of behaviourally distinct policies with novelty rejection. Prereg section 1 has cells, environment fingerprints and epochs, and section 8 keeps actor cells separate. The compliance linter keeps dev-specific content out of Skills. Section 11 says to widen the environment-shift variance when |z| > 2 and to favour policies robust across dev conditions. Trajectories store every observation. Not covered: per-episode public-condition descriptors and any measure of 'robust across dev conditions', which section 11 refers to but nothing computes.
cards.rationale: The concern underneath the card is officially confirmed. packages.rst says the official evaluation dataset and parameters are unpublished and that dev behaviour, thresholds and event composition must not be assumed identical. Expert-review question 4 asks how the Skills adapt when environment settings change. The opponent-pool mechanism does not transfer literally: there are no opponents, we cannot control seeds, and we cannot sample evaluation conditions. What we can do cheaply is measure whether a policy's advantage is concentrated in a narrow set of public conditions. That measurement is diagnostic: it informs the section 11 tie-break, child generation and the video's robustness argument. Spending target episodes on artificial stress settings would not model the unknown evaluation set and cannot be justified at 20-80 episodes.
cards.experiment: Engineering change shared with P23's analyser, 0 sessions. Extract a public-condition descriptor per episode from trajectory.jsonl (and from the official runner's own logs for target runs). Fields: starting visible stats, count and timing of risk warnings, review-grade sequence, first-promotion month, exit cause and month, number of story events, and declared mode notes. Store it as JSON referenced by SHA-256; no game text goes into Git. Fix 2-3 coarse strata before any selection data. Examples: starting Health or Dignity above or below the published midpoint, and whether any risk warning appeared in the first half-year. Post-treatment strata are descriptive only. Report mean Y per policy by stratum with partial pooling, plus per-policy coverage. Use 1: flag fragile leaders whose advantage sits in one stratum, then generate a child to address it. Use 2: for the section 11 tie-break within delta/2, prefer the smaller between-stratum spread. Use 3: evidence for video question 4. Strata never appear in Skills. Hypothesis kept in the bank: a stress epoch under perturbed engine settings (for example a different CAREER_EMULATOR_MONTHLY_EVENT_LIMIT). It would run in its own environment fingerprint, never pooled. Trigger: two finalists within delta/2, or an official score with |z| > 2 against prediction. Then about 4 target episodes per finalist, as an estimate only.

source_check.notes: C15 (ALE-Agent, AHC058) is supported by Sakana's report. The agent placed first, with comments from the problem author and the AHC overseer and a link to the official standings, which I did not open. It used greedy construction, then simulated annealing with large-neighbourhood operations, and the report credits the large neighbourhoods with a significant part of the score. It also used a 'virtual power' heuristic that values machines not yet producing as if they already were. That contribution is not measured: the report says which components mattered remains future research. About 4,773 calls (2,654 GPT-5.2 and 2,119 Gemini 3 Pro) and about USD 1,300 are confirmed. Mis-citation: C05 (Flat Neurons) describes no in-game investment. The nearest thing is a training-time entropy-schedule reset that causes short dips but ends stronger, which is not a policy mechanism. A better in-game example the card misses is C03, Lux S2: ry_andy pushed lichen growth early to generate power later.

cards.already_covered: Fully covered by design. Family f2-invest-early (invest-then-convert) builds Skill and Network first and switches to CONVERT on state or feedback evidence, not the calendar. It is horizon-aware through the published six-month review cadence, and its predicted behaviour and refutation are written down. Prereg section 3.2 uses prefix-complete data, section 9 allows no partial proxies without validation, and dormancy needs at least 4 terminal episodes. Method-decision section 3 problem B covers KM/RMST and crossing curves. The synthetic testbed has a late-benefit lever (promotion needs Skill and Network) and invest_build/invest_deliver parameters.
cards.rationale: Virtual power is a numeric evaluation heuristic inside a deterministic optimiser with a known model. Its number cannot be imported: the rules ban unpublished formulas and thresholds. Its idea is already a family. In this game, promotion plausibly depends on accumulated capability, so the late-benefit structure is credible. That makes F2 the family most likely to be wrongly discarded on interim data, which the protocol already prevents. A separate P11 arm would duplicate F2. The value of this card is to insist that F2 stays in the initial target race, even if budget forces cutting families to three or four.
cards.experiment: No separate arm. Shaping: keep F2 in the first target race. If families must be cut, keep the three poles of this axis: F1 (balanced), F2 (invest then convert) and F4 (deliver first). Diagnostics from the shared analyser: per-month Level, Skill and Network curves; P(survive to months 24, 36 and 48) against F4 and F1; and F2's manipulation check (the switch follows the listed evidence, not a fixed month). Triggered follow-up, target only: if F2 trails on Y while its completed episodes reach a higher Level at month 48 than F4, or its switch never fires, spawn one refine child that rewords the switch conditions. Race it against frozen F2 on Y = 0.8Q + 0.1E with delta = 4. At sigma about 12, n is about 81 per arm for power, so within this week's budget the result is a posterior estimate; it uses sections 3, 4, 6 and 9. Refutation, as the card states: if F2 shows no terminal Y advantage after its share of blocks, it goes dormant. An investment story is never an excuse. Gate: jiuwenswarm-target.

source_check.notes: The sources are real and the placings check out. Two Sigma confirms reCurs3 first in Halite II, and DeNA reports HandyRL first among 875 teams. But they do not support 'less defensive' play. Halite II's winner was more cautious in several mechanisms: a planet-safety check before docking, after he saw ships destroyed soon after docking; a health multiplier that seeks roughly 2:1 trades; a conservative model of enemy moves; and a survival mode for lost 4-player games. He was more aggressive only in focusing attacks on docked ships. In HandyRL, the RL agent's early deaths came from naive trust learned in self-play. The fix was MCTS lookahead, which also chose risk-avoiding play early by assuming weaker opponents. The blog's remark that a fearless AI sometimes judges risky moments better is generic. The sources support calibrated risk with explicit consequence checks. The 'less defensive' framing is the teammate's own counterintuitive hypothesis.

cards.already_covered: Covered by family design. f4-visible-delivery makes opportunities the default, steps back only when a qualitative wellbeing floor is breached, and calls Defuse legacy risk after a risk warning. That is exactly 'prioritise opportunities without public evidence of urgency, keep responding to real warnings'. f1-steady-balance is the defensive comparator and f3-feedback-reactive is the warning-driven contrast. The m3 teammate text explicitly avoids indefinite defensive play. Y includes the cap of E at 50 for early exits.
cards.rationale: Being less defensive pays only if the Q it gains outweighs its added early-exit risk. Here an early exit freezes Q at the state at exit and caps E at 50, which costs up to 5 Y-points on top of lost Q. The official rules also tell teams to design for consistent performance across repeated runs. F4 against F1 already tests this axis at family level in the initial race. Isolating 'defensiveness' alone would need an arm whose text differs only in the recovery trigger. At about 81 episodes per arm for delta = 4, it cannot be powered this week, and it is only worth an estimate if the specific symptom appears.
cards.experiment: No separate arm now. Triggered child, target only. Trigger: for two consecutive blocks the leader is a balanced or defensive family (F1, F3 or M3) with a high completion rate but a weak career-level and review profile ('survives without progress' in the episode profiles). Intervention: a child of the leader whose recovery rule fires only on warnings or lower-range readings, not at the first sign of a falling trend. Everything else is byte-identical. Comparator: the frozen leader. Outcome: Y; delta = 4; sigma about 12, so this is an estimate within the racing budget (at least 4 terminal episodes before any dormancy). Refutation: the child's posterior mean is below the parent's; the gain disappears under the Bayesian-bootstrap refit or depends on a few high-Q runs (compare the median and a trimmed mean); or its higher early-exit rate offsets the Q gain through the E cap. Prereg sections 3, 4, 6 (generation share and dormancy) and 11. Gate: jiuwenswarm-target.

source_check.notes: C03 (ry_andy, Lux S2) is supported. He pushed lichen growth early and kept doing so. His 'ice conflicts' deliberately accepted worse factory spots to deny an opponent ice; he credits it as what kept him competitive, and admits it failed against a rival with flexible ice transport. C09 (Halite II) is supported. In 4-player games a state mask focuses the bot on one target player, with exceptions near its own planets. The author says removing it always made results worse, an informal, uncontrolled ablation, while also admitting the mask's blind spots. Restricting attacks to docked ships also gave a marked improvement. Mis-citation: C15 (AHC058) is about investment valuation and large-neighbourhood search, not concentration on one dimension. Both supported cases are adversarial games where focus pays through snowballing against an opponent.

cards.already_covered: Covered by family design. f2 concentrates by stage: BUILD then CONVERT, with an exit back to BUILD. f4 concentrates on Output, with the wellbeing floor as its urgency exception and exit. f3 concentrates on corrective action after C or D reviews and warnings. f1 is the 'balance every decision' comparator the card asks for. The initial race compares them.
cards.rationale: The winners' mechanism (focus one opponent, snowball) has no analogue in a single-agent career. Here the ending weights six dimensions, and persistent weakness in any published failure direction ends the run, so concentration has a built-in collateral risk. A temporary dominant priority with urgency exceptions and an exit condition is still a reasonable hypothesis, and F2 and F4 already embody it. A separate family would add an arm without adding a new question.
cards.experiment: No separate arm. Triggered child, target only. Trigger: F1 leads, or is within delta/2 of the lead, while review grades stay flat and promotions are rare ('balance without progress'). Intervention: F1 plus one rule. For one review cycle, the factor named by the latest review or warning feedback becomes the dominant priority, with urgency exceptions taken from F1's existing guards, and an exit at the next review or on a floor breach. Wording stays qualitative, with no month numbers. Comparator: frozen F1. Outcome: Y with delta = 4; an estimate at feasible n. Diagnostics: whether the named bottleneck improved, and exit shares from the non-focus dimensions. Refutation: collateral exits rise enough to offset the gain, or the named bottleneck does not move. Prereg sections 4, 6 and 10 (it is a mode: compare with the never and always variants if any claim is made). Gate: jiuwenswarm-target.

source_check.notes: The sources do show winners using context-triggered modes on visible state. In Lux S2, units hold non-permanent roles and goals whose validity is re-checked every step (C03). Kore's 'abandon' pattern triggers when a shipyard cannot be defended, and the version that took the lead was named after it; the author makes no causal claim (C07). Halite II has an early-game mode and a 4-player survival override (C09). The survival override fires only when all its conditions hold, including more than 60 turns elapsed, and it is terminal: it never tries to recover. None of these sources discusses survivor bias or how often a context is reached. None says a globally bad candidate can supply a useful mode. That statistical content is the lab's own, matching the prereg section 10 design and the errata on problem C.

cards.already_covered: Mostly covered. Prereg section 10: complete policies against never and always arms, accepted only if P(mu_switch > max(never, always) + delta) >= 0.8 in fresh games; micro-randomised switches at quarter starts with p = 0.5; a placebo switch month drawn from 5-12; spurious if the effect appears only among survivors; calendar arms are diagnostic and never shipped. Method-decision section 3 problem C and the Recombine operator (modules from different branches) also apply. The synthetic testbed has switch_rule none/calendar/state/feedback with switch_month = 8. Not covered: a reach-rate metric (share of episodes that reach the mode's context, and when). Decision-point data exist only in the trajectory act notes and metadata, not in a registry table, although the errata ask for one.
cards.rationale: The survivor risk is acute in this game. Scripted floors exit at a median of 6-7.5 months, so any late-run mode is observed only in survivors. But the protection already exists: complete-policy racing from fresh games plus section 10. On the target, a within-episode randomised switch is not available without changing the official runner, so only complete-policy arms are possible there. Section 10's three-arm acceptance needs roughly 3 x 81 episodes, which is infeasible this week, so any specialist would be shipped only as a posterior estimate inside a complete policy. The card earns a slot only when its trigger fires. Its one cheap addition, reach rate, belongs in the shared episode-profile analyser.
cards.experiment: Trigger: trace analysis suggests a rule tied to a month or to 'after the first review'; or a mode's benefit appears only in episodes that survive to its context; or the synthetic or audit data show a mode firing at the same decision point regardless of state (aliasing). Action when triggered: write the mode as a state- or feedback-triggered continuation inside the leader's complete policy, with the prefix byte-identical. Race it against the frozen leader from fresh games. Report the unconditional Y and the reach rate P(context reached), with outcomes conditional on reaching the context as diagnostics only. Never ship the calendar version. Any claim needs section 10 (never and always arms plus placebo); otherwise the result is labelled an estimate. Delta = 4, sigma about 12. Method check, synthetic only: if the planned synthetic comparison has no problem-C cell, add one. Ground truth: the state-driven benefit is aliased with month 8 in typical games. Compare naive survivor-conditioned analysis, complete-policy racing and section 10 on false and true acceptance rates. Cost: CPU minutes. Gate: synthetic is open; jiuwenswarm-target for the policy arm.

combinations: One engineering change serves P23, P24 and P35, and provides the diagnostics P10, P11 and P12 need. Build an episode-profile analyser over the existing trajectory.jsonl files (and the official runner's own logs for target runs). It extracts public start state, exit cause and month, review grades, promotions, warning-to-defuse lag, declared-mode notes and first arrival at each mode (reach rate), rejected actions and tokens per month. At every promotion it emits a regression card against the frozen champion. It is descriptive only, never gates a decision, uses 0 game sessions, and commits no game text.

P10, P11 and P12 are one axis, defensive/balanced against deliver-first against invest-then-convert, and families F1, F4 and F2 already span it. A factorial is not warranted: the interaction is not the question, and a 2x2 at about 81 episodes per cell for delta = 4 is far beyond 20-80 target episodes. If the family list must be trimmed, keep all three poles of this axis.

P11 with P35: F2's CONVERT stage is a contextual specialist. Its manipulation check (the switch follows evidence, not a month) and its reach rate are the P35 and section 10 aliasing checks applied to F2. Run them from the shared analyser, not as a new arm.

P23 with P24: diversify the regression diagnostics across public strata and actors, and rotate them. This avoids what Halite II's author found, that head-to-head testing against previous versions alone became unreliable.

Submission interplay: Stage 1 is the maximum over scored versions, so P23's 'never regress' is not a Stage 1 constraint. The frozen champion matters for the final ZIP (expert review, per-version document quality) and for confirmation claims under section 7; P24's stratum spread is a section 11 tie-breaker.
review.group_summary: None of the six risk-investment-evaluation cards earns its own target experiment. The protocol needs roughly 81 episodes per arm to resolve delta = 4 at sigma about 12, against 20-80 target episodes this week, and each card is already built into CareerLab. P10 is family F4 (deliver first, with a floor and a response to warnings) against F1. P11 is family F2 (invest then convert, with protection against problem B). P12 is covered by F2 and F4 against F1. P23 is covered by prereg sections 6, 7 and 11. P24 is covered by the archive's diversity rules and environment epochs. P35 is covered by section 10. Decisions: P23 and P24 are infrastructure_change_now, through one shared episode-profile analyser with a regression card against a frozen champion. It runs on existing trajectories with 0 sessions, and it supplies the expert-review video's questions 2 and 4 (what earlier logs showed; how robust the Skills are) and the section 11 tie-break. P10, P11 and P12 are fold_into_family_design; F2 must stay in the first target race, and each card has a written trigger for a single refine child. P35 is hypothesis_only with a trigger, plus a reach-rate metric in the analyser. Source review: the placings and core mechanisms check out for Flat Neurons, Kore, ry_andy, Halite II, HandyRL and AHC058. I read the Kaggle pages in the built-in browser and Halite II through a Wayback snapshot, because the live site refused connections. Overclaims found: (1) P10's sources show calibrated or even more cautious risk handling, not reduced defensiveness. (2) P11 cites C05, which has no in-game investment; Lux S2's early lichen push is a better example. (3) P12 cites C15, which is not about concentration. (4) The C08 Halite 2020 harness's promote-and-evolve branch is disabled in the committed config, which runs 7 deterministic seeded games against a fixed pool. (5) The host and runner-up comments claimed for S05 and S10 are not visible. (6) AHC058's virtual power is cited, but its contribution is unmeasured. Two findings run against the cards' framing: Halite II's author found that testing against previous versions alone became unreliable, and the official docs confirm the evaluation dataset and parameters differ from dev, so robustness counts as a measured diagnostic, not a tunable target.

verdicts.proposed_decision: infrastructure_change_now
verdicts.reason: Source re-check. I re-read the Flat Neurons writeup in a rendering browser. It confirms a frozen best-so-far teacher with a KL loss and a frozen pool of older opponents. The author's comment says the teacher was updated every 100-200M-step iteration, but only when the new model was better, and the pool reached 15-20 models. I fetched ttvand's main_rule_based.py; its git blob is 9230c0e, which matches. It has NUM_GAMES=7, deterministic_games=True, seed 0, play_fixed_pool_only=True and previous-pool/evaluation games set to x0, so the 0.6 promotion branch is inactive. The reviewer is right on all of this. The Kore writeup confirms two weeks and 26 updates from V92 to V118. Two corrections to the reviewer's notes. (i) The comments are visible once the page renders. S05 shows the Competition Host (Stone Tao) congratulating first place. S10 shows 49 comments, including basilisk1337 (2nd). 'Both pages show 0 comments' was a rendering artefact. (ii) The Halite II author says local tests against previous versions became 'increasingly inaccurate and pointless' and that he wanted more diversity in his local pool. 'Non-transitive matchups' is the reviewer's own inference. The reviewer also missed evidence that supports the coverage claim. Flat Neurons evaluated its stronger model inside the live submission (85/15 per match, logged), and Halite II calls online per-version statistics 'by far the #1 way' to evaluate changes. Both winners anchored promotion on the real evaluator, which is what CareerLab's target anchoring does. Neither mechanism transfers further: each version gets only three official runs, and there is no per-run arm logging. Why the decision holds: (a) prereg-v1 section 11 already requires comparing each official score with its prediction (|z|>2), but careerlab/store.py has no field for a submitted version, its predicted score or its official result. That record must exist before the 27 Oct cutoff. It can be a 'submission'/'champion' kind in the existing decisions table, with no schema change. (b) careerlab/report.py already reports completion and RMST48 per cell, so the regression card is a small addition: exit causes, ending dimensions, grade sequence and tokens per month, shown against the champion. It feeds video question 2, which I checked in competition-rules. Conditions. The automatic '>=2 SE worse failure family' scan covers about 6-8 exit or dimension families at n of about 4-10 per arm, with no multiplicity control. Only each policy's pre-declared manipulation checks (predicted_behaviour/refutation in policy.json, e.g. F1 'fewer health/dignity eliminations', F4 'higher health-direction risk') may raise flags; everything else is labelled exploratory. The P1 trajectories (0 completions, median 6-7.5 months) test code paths only, not whether the card is useful.

verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only
verdicts.reason: The reviewer's source check is right. DeNA: about 16M self-play games, then about 3M against past models and colliding agents, which fixed naive cooperation. Flat Neurons: an opponent pool against overfitting to its own style. Neither mechanism transfers, because there are no opponents. The proposed infrastructure cannot do what it claims, for four reasons. (1) I hashed the first observation of all 150 P1 dev episodes in /Users/alejandrotreny/careerlab-data/huawei/runs/pilo-*/trajectory.jsonl, using our own outputs only. All 150 are identical: status, event, choices and feedback, with health 5, dignity 5, skill 1, network 1, L1, wealth 1. So the proposed pre-treatment stratum 'starting Health or Dignity above or below the midpoint' is constant on dev. (2) The other example stratum, 'any risk warning in the first half-year', is post-treatment: F3 defuses risk and F4 takes it on. Stratifying a policy comparison on it conditions on the outcome path. (3) With 20-80 target episodes spread over 6-8 families, each policy-by-stratum cell holds about 1-5 episodes. An interaction needs roughly 4x the main-effect n (about 320 per arm at delta=4, sigma=12), so 'flag fragile leaders whose advantage sits in one stratum' cannot be estimated. (4) Use 2 (break the section 11 tie within delta/2 by the smaller between-stratum spread) changes a frozen rule. prereg-v1 section 11 says to prefer the simpler, lower-token policy, and any change needs v2. What remains (warning timing, grade sequence, exit cause and month, environment fingerprint) is already in P23's analyser and prereg section 1, at no extra cost. Keep in the bank. Trigger: an official score with |z|>2 against prediction (section 11 already says to widen shift variance and favour robust policies), or reaching the top ten with expert-review question 4 to answer. Action when triggered: write prereg v2 defining a robustness criterion, then run a stress epoch under perturbed engine settings in its own environment fingerprint, never pooled. That epoch also needs a lab/gate.json update, because real-dev is authorised only for the official runner engine settings.

verdicts.proposed_decision: fold_into_family_design
verdicts.reason: Sources checked. sakana.ai/ahc058 describes 'virtual power' but reports no measured contribution for it, gives 2,654 GPT-5.2 and 2,119 Gemini 3 Pro calls and about USD 1,300, and says that identifying which elements mattered 'remains an important research task'. Flat Neurons has no in-game investment, only the entropy-reset training dips. ry_andy's Lux S2 writeup does have it: 'push lichen growth early and often to generate as much power as possible'. The reviewer's mis-citation note is correct. Transfer is backed by the published rules: rules.rst says 'Promotion assessment considers factors including Skill, Network, and Output. Requirements increase with level.' A late-benefit structure is therefore plausible, and F2 (invest-then-convert) implements it compliantly: the switch is on state or feedback, and its horizon uses only the published 48-month length and 6-month cadence. The fold has a concrete, free consequence that justifies the label: F2, and the F1/F2/F4 poles, stay in the initial target race if budget forces cuts. The n of about 81 per arm (9*144/16) is right. One correction to the triggered follow-up. 'F2 trails on Y while its completed episodes reach a higher Level at month 48 than F4' conditions on survivors, which is the pattern prereg section 10 calls spurious. Use unconditional measures before spawning the refine child: Level at exit over all episodes, P(survive to months 24/36/48) and RMST. Keep the manipulation-check trigger (the switch never fires) as written.

verdicts.proposed_decision: fold_into_family_design
verdicts.reason: I re-checked the sources. The reviewer is right that they support calibrated risk, not 'less defensive' play. The Halite II post-mortem (archived copy, fetched) adds a planet-safety check after seeing docked ships destroyed a few turns after docking. It multiplies ally health by 1.9 to seek trades of at least 2:1, predicts enemy grouping conservatively, and uses a terminal 4-player survival mode. Its only gain from aggression was attacking docked ships only, which gave a 'remarkable improvement'. The DeNA blog says MCTS made survival look more valuable and avoided early risk; the 'fearless AI' remark is generic. The fold is acceptable because the card's axis is already tested by the F4-vs-F1 contrast in the initial race, at no extra arm cost, and the triggered child is well specified (Y, delta=4, E-cap offset in the refutation). Condition: F4 predates the card. Its policy.json says 'initial family seed', and grep finds no playbook or card reference anywhere in lab/policies-src. Do not record idea_origin playbook:P10/C09/C10 on F4, and do not cite these winners as support for less-defensive play in the design docs or video, because they show the opposite.

verdicts.proposed_decision: fold_into_family_design
verdicts.reason: Sources verified in a rendering browser. ry_andy's 'ice conflicts' deliberately took worse spawns to deny ice ('the only thing that kept me competitive') and did not work against flg's flexible ice transport. The Halite II mask: 'every time I tried removing this masking, my bot performed worse overall' (informal ablation). Both are about focusing on an opponent, so transfer is weak, as the reviewer says, and the C15 mis-citation is real. No arm is spent; F2/F4 vs F1 already contrast concentration with balance. One refinement: the proposed triggered child (F1 plus 'the factor named by the latest review becomes the dominant priority for one cycle, exit at next review') is almost exactly F3's existing 'Weak review plan'. That plan names the factor, aims the main action at it until the next review, and changes factor if the grade is still weak. F1 already has 'after a C or D review, add Output-producing actions until the next review'. If the trigger fires, build the child with the Recombine operator (F1 core plus F3's weak-review module), record F3 as a parent, and read the existing F1-vs-F3 race result first. Do not write new P12 text. The trigger ('balance without progress') should use unconditional measures (grades and level over all episodes), not survivors only.

verdicts.proposed_decision: hypothesis_only
verdicts.reason: Sources verified. ry_andy: roles and goals are re-validated every step. Kore: an abandon pattern when a shipyard cannot be defended, and 'V127abandonrescuecollideattack' took the lead with no causal claim. Halite II: the survival override needs all conditions, including more than 60 turns, and 'is a terminal state'. None discusses reach rate or survivor bias; that content is the lab's own, as the reviewer says. The trigger has not been observed yet. There are no target traces, and no synthetic problem-C results exist: there is no lab/reports, no careerlab/search, and tests/ never references calendar8 or state_switch. Correction: the reviewer's conditional 'add a problem-C cell if the synthetic comparison lacks one' is moot. careerlab/synthetic/policy.py DESIGNED already contains state_switch, calendar8 and feedback_switch, labelled 'Problem C', so the planned synthetic comparison covers it. New supporting evidence: all 150 P1 dev episodes start from an identical first observation (hashed, own outputs). In every dev episode before a first promotion, calendar month, months at the current level and reviews elapsed are therefore exactly aliased. Any timing-shaped rule taken from traces should be treated as calendar-aliased by default and rewritten as a state or feedback condition. No experiment could change a decision now: calendar variants are never shipped, and section 10's three-arm acceptance (about 3x81 episodes) is infeasible this week. Reach rate goes into P23's shared analyser as a descriptive field.

source_check.notes: C01 is supported. The AutoAscend README says 'simulate' mode resumes from an existing results JSON and skips seeds already simulated, so no seed runs twice. C08 is weaker. ttvand's main_rule_based.py re-feeds past config scores from a CSV to a skopt optimiser (opt.tell), which is resuming optimiser state. I saw no deduplication logic. Seed-based deduplication does not transfer, because we have no seeds or replay; here a duplicate means the same job, replicate or content.

cards.already_covered: Mostly covered for scripted actors. careerlab/store.py has policy ids from content hashes, jobs that are UNIQUE on (policy, actor, env, purpose, replicate, attempt), lease, recover(), requeue_interrupted(), and ingest() that never scores an interrupted attempt. careerlab/scheduler.py has recover() and resume_scripted(), which observe first. careerlab/episode.py writes results atomically and classifies interruptions. prereg-v1.md section 3.3-3.5 covers inclusion. findings.md records the kill -9 pilot. Gaps I found in the code: (a) Scheduler._beat (scheduler.py L60-69, L103, L159) runs only after an episode completes, and owner_alive treats a beat older than 120 s as dead. Claude episodes run up to 7,200 s (claude_cli.py L39). A recover() from another process during a long LLM or target episode would therefore mark a live job interrupted, and a future resume for LLM actors could play the same session twice. mark_running also stores the scheduler pid, not the worker pid. (b) max_continues=3 (claude_cli.py L38), but the participation runner uses MAX_CONTINUATIONS = 20 (local-runs/official-runner/career_sim_runner/ws_client.py L19). Episodes the official runner would continue are classified interrupted, which biases against long games (problem B). (c) trajectory_path and its SHA cover only stream-0.jsonl (claude_cli.py L230), so continuation streams are not hashed. (d) bundle_hash uses exact bytes (store.py L53), but the official rules treat formatting, renaming and metadata-only changes as content-identical. (e) There is no recover or resume path for target-runner jobs.
cards.rationale: Target episodes are the scarcest resource this week. Losing or duplicating one, or wrongly classifying a long successful game as interrupted, costs money and biases selection against late-benefit policies. The fixes are engineering with clear pass/fail tests, so an experiment would not change any decision. The content-identity gap also affects submission. A version that differs from an already-scored one only in formatting would not be rescored, and that cutoff would be wasted.
cards.experiment: Not an experiment. Fixes to make before any Claude or target episode: (1) Each owner writes its heartbeat periodically (every 30 s or less, as an asyncio task, to a file per owner or a registry table), independent of completions. Store the worker or runner pid as well. recover() treats a job as running while that pid is alive or its lease has not expired. resume refuses a session whose job still has a live owner. Unit test: a fake actor that sleeps 10 minutes, plus a concurrent `careerlab recover`, must leave the job running. (2) Set the Claude worker's continuation cap to 20, as in the participation runner, or record the difference in the actor config. (3) Target jobs use the official runner's own --continue path, flagged 'continued' (the same as the official runner does). An agent process restarted on the same game session is flagged 'restarted' and goes only into a sensitivity analysis. Write this as a prereg v2 amendment before any target data exist. (4) Hash every stream-k.jsonl and the runner's events JSONL. (5) Add a normalised content hash (whitespace and markdown formatting stripped, file names and metadata ignored). Use it to reject formatting-only children, which would split an arm's budget, and to refuse to submit a version content-identical to an already-scored one. (6) Recovery only checks that the database file exists and calls observe through the official tools. It never reads the simulation database.

source_check.notes: C14 is supported, and it is the only real scaling probe among the cited cases. Psyho reran with a 10x time limit, which 'increased the score by 25-30%'. He concluded that simulation speed was the limit and optimised the simulation code, from about 120K to about 1.5M simulations. That was a deterministic local solver, not a noisy search over policies. C15's figures are accurate: GPT-5.2 2,654 calls plus Gemini 3 Pro 2,119 calls = 4,773, about USD 1,300. But the report only asserts 'inference-time scaling' and shows no curve of result against budget, so it does not support 'measure the discovery curve'. It says itself that which components caused the result is still an open research question. C16's 320 trials for about USD 60 and the 6.5x/10x solver speedups are accurate, but that was one fixed-budget experiment, not a scaling test. AtCoder confirms Psyho finished first.

cards.already_covered: Partly. method-decision.md section 2.3 covers sample size from observed variance and section 2.5 keeps best-of-N and refine-the-leader as equal-budget baselines. prereg-v1.md covers planning n (section 5), stagnation (section 6) and the budget split with the rule for fewer than 20 episodes (section 12). The synthetic method comparison is planned but not built: careerlab/search does not exist yet. careerlab/synthetic/game.py provides fast_episode, truth and throughput. Nothing yet measures how the quality of the chosen policy changes with total target budget, or how many families to enter at a given budget.
cards.rationale: In our setting the question is not 'more workers'. It is how many target episodes to buy (a team decision still pending) and how many families to race. Both are allocation and statistics questions, so the synthetic testbed's known ground truth can answer them. I ran a quick pure-Python normal-means calculation (not the game, not a model): sigma 12 Y, independent candidates, equal allocation, choose the best sample mean. At K=4, doubling B from 40 to 80 raises the chosen policy's true value by only about 0.3-0.4 Y. Going from K=4 to K=8 at B=40 adds +0.1 Y when the spread between families tau is 3 and +1.2 Y when tau is 6, while P(chosen within Delta of the best entered) falls from 0.91 to about 0.78. If the real racing code confirms this, spend beyond about 40 selection episodes is poor value, and more distinct families or confirmation is the better use. That bears directly on the self-funded budget and on the plan to race 6-8 families in method section 7.
cards.experiment: Add this to the planned synthetic method comparison as a factorial, because the interaction between method and budget is the question. Intervention: the full CareerLab racing procedure (prereg sections 4 and 6: blocks, top-two Thompson sampling, partial pooling, dormancy and audits, prefix-complete decisions) at total target-equivalent budgets B in {20, 40, 80, 160}, with K in {2, 4, 6, 8} candidate policies. A 'diversity' arm puts half of each block's slots into new candidates, standing in for the card's representation-change comparator. Comparators: equal allocation with best-of-N pick at the same B, and the B=40 base. Use designed-family candidate sets tuned so per-episode SD is about 12 Y and the spread between policies tau is in {3, 6}, plus a heavy-tailed variant. Apply prereg section 12's split: 15% pilot, 55% selection, 30% confirmation. Outcomes: the chosen policy's true Y from truth() with n=20,000, simple regret, P(within Delta=4 of the best entered), and the error between posterior predicted and true score (winner's curse). The unit is a complete search, with 300-500 searches per cell. Estimated cost: a few million fast synthetic episodes; measure throughput() first, and I expect at most a few CPU-hours on this Mac. It needs careerlab/search. Decision rule: if doubling B from 40 to 80 at the best K gains less than Delta/4 = 1 Y under both tau settings, cap the target selection budget at about 40 and put the rest into candidate diversity and confirmation. If it gains Delta/2 = 2 Y or more under either setting, recommend buying more target episodes. Choose K for R2 at the affordable B. Refutation: my prior of diminishing returns is wrong if the racing code reaches 2 Y or more per doubling. Prereg sections used: 4, 5, 6, 12; method sections 2.3 and 2.5. Gate: synthetic scripted actors, allowed with no cap. Caveat: tau for the real game is unknown, so after the target pilot rerun the relevant cell with the measured sigma. The synthetic result is about allocation, not game content.

review.group_summary:
None of the six infrastructure and jury cards justifies spending target episodes. P34 gets one synthetic experiment, added to the planned method comparison. P36, P33, P31 and P30 become engineering or process changes, and P03 goes into the family design.

**Source review.** Most cited evidence is self-reported by the winners, and several card-to-case links are overclaims:
- Psyho's 10x-time probe (C14) is the only real scaling test. It was run on a deterministic solver.
- ALE-Agent asserts that more inference spend helps but never measures it.
- The Huawei Ireland claim (1st in the algorithm section, 3rd overall because of the presentation) comes only from the team itself.
- AutoAscend's action abstraction answers a NetHack keystroke problem that our atomic MCP choices do not have.
- AutoAscend's resume and seed deduplication is real, but its deduplication relies on seeds, which we do not have.
- The Kore writeup (rendered by JavaScript) and the Halite II post-mortem (connection refused) could not be verified today.

**What is already covered.** Much of what these cards propose already exists in CareerLab:
- observe-before-retry in careerlab/mcp_client.py;
- the registry, leases, recovery and scripted resume in careerlab/store.py and careerlab/scheduler.py;
- the bench and per-tool timing;
- hypothesis, prediction and refutation fields in each policy.json;
- the hygiene line 'if success is false, observe' in every family Skill.

**Concrete defects found while checking coverage (P33):**
- The scheduler writes its heartbeat only after an episode completes, and treats a heartbeat older than 120 s as dead (scheduler.py L60-69). Claude episodes can run up to 7,200 s (claude_cli.py L39), so a recover() from another process would mark a live LLM or target job as interrupted.
- The Claude worker allows 3 continuations (claude_cli.py L38), while the participation runner allows 20 (ws_client.py L19). Long games are therefore wrongly counted as interrupted, which biases against late-benefit policies.
- Only stream-0.jsonl is hashed (claude_cli.py L230).
- Policy ids are byte hashes (store.py L53), while the official rules treat formatting-only changes as content-identical. A formatting-only version could waste a cutoff and would also split an arm's budget.

**Priorities:**
1. **P36, now.** The first cutoff is in about 36 hours. presentation.mp4 is required, and there is no solution/ directory yet. Video question 2 needs logs from an earlier version, which makes the target pilot urgent for evidence as well as for budgeting.
2. **P33 fixes**, before any LLM or target episode.
3. **P34 synthetic study.** It informs how many target episodes to buy and how many families to race. A quick normal-means check (sigma 12 Y) suggests that going from 40 to 80 selection episodes adds only about 0.3-0.4 Y, while more distinct families matter more when they differ by a lot.
4. **P03:** add the error/no-reply clause to the shared execution block of every family, with identical wording.
5. **P31:** profile tokens and time per component from the official runner's own logs during the pilot. This matters because E is scored. Never profile the engine process itself.
6. **P30:** require a diagnosis record for every child policy.

The five non-experiment cards each carry the trigger that would escalate them. No game, model or file was run or edited for this review; the only computation was a pure-Python Monte Carlo of normal means.

verdicts.reason: I verified the code. _beat runs only after an episode completes (scheduler.py L103, L159), and owner_alive treats a beat older than 120 s as dead (L69). The problem is worse than the review says. There is one heartbeat file shared by all schedulers (L58, data_dir/scheduler.heartbeat.json), and cmd_run and cmd_resume call recover() first (cli.py L130, L151). So any second scheduler overwrites the owner and makes the first scheduler's live jobs look dead. recover() then marks them interrupted (store.py L199-213), and resume_scripted can replay a live session. The scheduler has no target path at all; official_runner.run_target_episode is unwired. Two corrections. First, the reviewer's fix 3 conflates two things: the runner's automatic in-drive continuations (ws_client.py MAX_CONTINUATIONS=20, counted inside one StreamCollector) and the `play --continue` CLI restart. The restart reuses load_last_output_dir() and rewrites score_report.json, with token_usage from the new collector only (headless_play.py ~L124-160), and _from_report picks reports[-1] by mtime. A restarted episode would therefore under-report tokens and inflate E. Second, the review missed this: _from_report labels 'max_continuations' and timeout endings 'interrupted', so they are never scored. These are policy-caused non-completions. The rules score early exits ('An early exit still receives one'), and E is 0 when there is no survival length. Dropping these runs biases selection toward stalling or slow, verbose policies. Prereg section 3.6 would also push the target timeout above the official 7200 s (constants.py DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_S, TargetConfig.timeout_s). The fixes are cheap engineering with pass/fail tests, so no experiment is needed.

verdicts.proposed_decision: infrastructure_change_now: add a small normal-means budget planner next to required_n in careerlab/stats.py. Given sigma, a tau estimate and B_total, it returns expected regret, P(within Delta) by K, and the feasibility bound K <= floor(0.55*B_total/4) from the dormancy minimum. Use it now to set the number of R2 families: about 2 at B_total=20 and about 5 at B_total=40; method section 7's '6-8 families' needs B_total of about 60 or more. Rerun it after the target pilot with the measured sigma and the first-block tau. Do not build a separate 4x4x3 synthetic factorial. Run the already-planned racing vs best-of-N vs refine-leader comparison (method section 2.5) only at the realistic operating points, B_sel 11-44 and K 3-6. Keep the full budget-scaling study as a hypothesis, triggered by evidence of a heavy-tailed candidate distribution on the target (one family's first-block mean far above the others, implying tau > 10).
verdicts.reason: Sources hold. Psyho: 10x time gave +25-30% and 'the main bottleneck was the simulation code'. AHC058: 2,654 + 2,119 calls, about USD 1,300, with no budget curve and 'remains an important research task'. I reproduced the reviewer's numbers with 20k-rep normal means: at K=4, going from B=40 to B=80 gains 0.38 Y (tau=3) and 0.41 Y (tau=6); K=4 to K=8 at B=40 gains +0.13 and +1.09; P(within Delta) falls from 0.91 to 0.78 and from 0.90 to 0.76. Those same numbers show the experiment cannot change the decision it targets. The gain from doubling B is bounded by the regret left at B=40: 1.16 or 0.97 at K=4 and 2.20 or 2.21 at K=8 under equal allocation, and racing leaves less. So the reviewer's 'gain of 2 Y or more per doubling, buy more' branch cannot fire for Gaussian tau <= 6; the result follows from the design. The K answer depends on tau, which the synthetic testbed fixes by assumption and cannot measure for the real game. The review also missed the constraint that actually binds. Prereg section 6 dormancy needs at least 4 terminal episodes per arm, and section 12 gives 55% of the budget to selection. At 20-80 target episodes, that is 11-44 selection episodes, so K=8 leaves 1-5 episodes per arm and racing degenerates to equal-allocation estimation. Money is not the binding constraint either: findings.md estimates about USD 0.6-1.2 per target episode, while wall-clock and the key matter more. The proposed factorial would need careerlab/search (it does not exist yet) and millions of synthetic episodes to produce a predetermined answer. A planner of a few dozen lines gives the decision-relevant table in seconds.
